In "Open and Distance eLearning: New Dimensions in Teaching, Learning, Research, and Extension for Higher Education Institutions," Grace Javier Alfonso and Primo G. Garcia examine the evolution of Open and Distance eLearning (ODeL) as a transformative framework for higher education. By integrating open learning, distance education, and e-learning, ODeL aims to promote social transformation and educational equity within a globalized, digital "network society." Using the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) as a case study, the authors trace the transition from print-based modules to fully online delivery models.

The study identifies several key dimensions of this shift. In instruction, teaching moves from faculty-centered to learner-centered, with instructors acting as facilitators rather than sole knowledge sources. Regarding resources, the use of Open Educational Resources (OER) and Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) democratizes knowledge through localized content. In research, digital environments allow for the use of learner analytics to study student behavior. In extension, ODeL enables universities to reach non-traditional learners, such as overseas workers, through scalable platforms.

The authors conclude that ODeL bridges the gap between academic rigor and accessibility by embracing mass participation and distributed expertise. To succeed, higher education institutions must establish legal frameworks, pursue industry and government partnerships, and utilize ICT infrastructure to become integrated knowledge hubs that foster lifelong learning.

The maiden issue of the International Journal on Open and Distance eLearning (IJODeL) introduces a platform dedicated to researching open learning, distance education, and eLearning. The editorial frames open and distance eLearning (ODeL) as a worldview for organizing research and practice. A lead article by Grace Javier Alfonso and Primo G. Garcia suggests that combining the philosophy of openness with distance education modalities can drive social transformation when integrated with university value systems. The journal advocates for using information and communication technologies, specifically open educational resources, to create a digital knowledge hub.

Several studies in this issue focus on mobile learning in Asia. Tuliao, Duldulao, Pagtaconan, and Galang present "iSuro," a mobile application designed for the Kindergarten curriculum to address the scarcity of learning materials. Miguel, Salvador, Guillen, and Nisperos explored mobile applications as supplementary tools for teaching Philippine history through "HiStorya," an interactive Android game. Findings indicated that the game's immersive and reward aspects motivated deeper study, while system-generated reports helped teachers evaluate student proficiency. Additionally, Ahmad Sobri Shuib and Muhammad Nidzam Yaakob found that pre-service teachers in Malaysia maintain positive attitudes toward using mobile technology for teaching and learning. Finally, Felix Librero provides a historical report on the 20-year development of the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU), detailing how the institution addressed online learning issues.

The study "Development of a Mobile Learning Application for Kindergarten: Process, Issues, and Challenges" investigates integrating Information and Communication Technology into early childhood education. Researchers identified several challenges in current Kindergarten environments, such as large class sizes, difficulty engaging students through traditional methods, the physical burden of heavy textbooks, and a scarcity of Department of Education learning materials.

Conducted within the Philippines' K to 12 Program, the research focused on the Cognitive/Intellectual Development domain using Mathematics. The researchers developed "iSuro," an Android-based mobile learning application designed to be an affordable, portable, and user-friendly complement to existing infrastructure. Using the Mobile-D Development Methodology, the team followed five phases: Explore, Initialize, Productionize, Stabilize, and System Test and Fix. The final iSuro application, developed using Eclipse 4.2 and an SQLite database, features a Learning Module with digital flipbooks and voice-overs, an Activity Module for skill evaluation, and an Assessment Module with rewards and leaderboards. Content is based on Kindergarten modules in the Iloco mother tongue.

User Acceptance Testing involving teachers, Kindergarteners, and parents indicated high satisfaction levels, with mean scores of 4.54, 4.37, and 4.43, respectively. The researchers conclude that mobile learning offers potential for personalization and mobility, making learners more productive and engaged. They recommend that schools in Ilocos Norte adopt the system and suggest adding more lessons and a language selection feature to increase accessibility.

The study "HiStorya: a Game Based Mobile Learning Application" addresses low student engagement in the Araling Panlipunan (AP) subject within the Philippine K-12 curriculum, where heavy emphasis on memorization often leads to boredom. Researchers aimed to develop an interactive Android mobile application as a supplementary tool for students and teachers, specifically focusing on Asian geography, history, culture, society, government, and economy.

Using an input-process-output model and the Digital Game-based Learning-Instructional Design (DGBL-ID) model, researchers gathered data through interviews with educators and surveys of Grade 8 students. Findings revealed that 90% of students own smart devices, 63% use Android, and 89% play games for one to two hours daily, with a preference for analogy, quiz, and memory games.

The resulting application, HiStorya, features three game categories aligned with curriculum assessment levels: a Quiz game for knowledge, a Memory game for process/skills, and an Analogy game for understanding. The app is organized into four levels corresponding to curriculum units, requiring correct answers to unlock new content. HiStorya includes a synchronization feature that uploads statistics to an online database, enabling a web-based module for teachers to monitor progress and administrators to manage content. A leaderboard was also implemented to foster competition. Researchers concluded that HiStorya is a motivating, relevant tool for both learning and instructional planning.

The study "Perception and Readiness of Pre-service Teachers on Mobile Learning" by Ahmad Sobri Shuib and Muhammad Nidzam Yaakob investigates how future educators in Malaysia view and prepare for integrating mobile technology into teaching. The research addresses the gap between the widespread use of smartphones and the limited formal mobile learning initiatives within teacher education institutes.

Using a quantitative design at the Institute of Teacher Education, Darul Aman Campus, the study surveyed 120 eighth-semester Bachelor of Teaching students. Data were collected through a validated 20-item Likert scale questionnaire. The findings indicate that pre-service teachers possess a high level of readiness and a positive perception toward mobile learning. Respondents showed a high willingness to use mobile devices for learning, specifically expressing very high willingness to use laptops and tablets to access the internet for information. They also showed high willingness to use smartphones to access the internet and download educational materials.

The authors conclude that implementing mobile learning in Malaysia is highly feasible and can serve as a cost-effective alternative to traditional methods by reducing expenses related to electricity, laboratories, and cabling. They recommend that institutions develop formal training modules and integrate mobile learning into the mainstream curriculum. Furthermore, the Ministry of Education should improve technological infrastructure and provide teachers with more devices and specialized training to support this shift.

In "ODeL at UPOU: Some Historical Antecedents: (How Did We Get Here, Anyway?)", Felix Librero traces the evolution of distance education at the University of the Philippines, from radio-based initiatives to the establishment of the U.P. Open University (UPOU). The development was driven by the need to provide quality higher education to underserved populations, address resource constraints in traditional campus-based instruction, and provide professional upgrading for teachers without requiring them to leave their jobs.

The history is rooted in two precursors at the University of the Philippines Los Baños: the "school on the air" (SOA) format via Radio DZLB, which provided systematic instruction to farmers and homemakers, and the Science Teaching Using Distance Instruction (STUDI) project, which addressed the shortage of qualified science teachers. Librero organizes this evolution into three stages: radio-based non-formal education, pilot distance instruction projects like STUDI, and the formal institutionalization of the UP Distance Education Program in 1992, which led to the creation of UPOU in 1995.

Findings indicate that SOA was effective for millions of learners, and STUDI proved distance education could successfully upgrade teacher competence. UPOU was designed to provide technical assistance and quality control across the UP system, targeting remote areas and non-traditional students. This evolution culminated in the transition from printed modules and radio to Open Distance e-Learning (ODeL), a model integrating open learning, distance education, and e-learning.
15:
This study investigates using mobile devices and Web 2.0 protocols to document and manage the indigenous knowledge systems (IKS) of rural communities in the Philippines. The research aimed to determine how mobile technology can empower marginalized groups to become active content providers, thereby increasing their social capital. Using a quasi-experimental action research design involving six indigenous communities, the researchers provided participants with GPRS-enabled mobile phones and training in mobile videography. A Web Content Management System was developed to serve as a secure repository for rich media.

The findings revealed a significant disconnect between technological potential and social realities. Although training provided technical proficiency, the participation rate in content submission was low. Several intervening variables hindered the implementation of an open-access system, including the need to honor indigenous belief systems that involve secrecy and ritual. Privacy concerns were paramount, as certain cultural practices are not intended for public viewing. Additionally, removing video clips from their original context can lead to inaccurate knowledge. The study also highlighted risks of prejudice from non-IP users and the potential for exploitation through bioprospecting and patenting.

The researchers concluded that while mobile technology can facilitate the capture of indigenous knowledge, "open access" cannot be applied universally. They proposed a conceptual model that incorporates inhibiting factors—such as belief systems, privacy, context, prejudice, misrepresentation, and legal protocols—into the framework of ICT4D.

In "Augmenting Learning Space in Post Graduate Courses in Literature Studies Through ODeL: A Critical Overview of NSOU Learning Praxis," Manan Kumar Mandal examines the implementation of Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL) within the School of Humanities at Netaji Subhas Open University (NSOU) in West Bengal, India. The study addresses the challenges of teaching advanced literature through distance education, which requires interactive spaces for dialectical deliberation, and the social skepticism regarding open university degrees.

Using an empirical analysis of NSOU's "blended learning" model, the author evaluates a system that combines traditional Open and Distance Learning (ODL) methods, such as Self-Instructional Materials (SIM) and Personal Contact Programmes (PCP), with ICT-enabled support via social networking platforms like Facebook and Google Chat. Findings indicate that this model significantly enhances learner engagement. SIMs serve as substitutes for face-to-face instruction, while PCPs maintain high attendance rates between 50% and 75%. Notably, virtual interaction via social media increased by approximately 50% between the 2014-15 and 2015-16 academic periods; for example, learners supported through online interaction in the Bengali course rose from approximately 500 to 1,200.

The author concludes that ODeL should extend rather than replace classical ODL pedagogy. By utilizing social media and existing resources to create interactive "learning spaces," open universities can improve academic accountability and provide inclusive higher education to diverse populations.

Ortiguero et al. (2021) examine the conceptualization of the University of the Future (UoF) through the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU). As the Fourth Industrial Revolution introduces disruptive technologies, higher education institutions must transition toward Education 4.0, focusing on agility and personalized, lifelong learning. Using a qualitative approach with thematic analysis, the researchers analyzed transcripts from five Virtual Roundtable Discussions involving faculty, students, staff, and alumni. These themes were superimposed onto five ODeL subsystems: course design, course delivery, instruction, student support, and management.

Findings within course design emphasized integrated curricula with micro-credentials and stackable credits. Course delivery focused on emerging technologies for flexible, personalized learning, while instruction required innovative functions like mentoring and collaboration with industry practitioners. Student support requires analytics-based responsiveness, and management must act as an integrator with a malleable structure. The study identified two major themes: "Peripheral Adjustments," which involve strengthening existing functions, and "Radical Transformation," which involves overhauling traditional dogmas like faculty tenure and administrative models.

The overarching theme is "Seamlessness," envisioning a permeable university with no rigid boundaries between itself and society. To become a UoF, UPOU must embrace flexibility, sustainability, and collaboration. The authors recommend a strategic, participative process to move away from "privileged seclusion" toward a responsive system integrated with global societal needs.

The article "Teacher Readiness for Online Teaching: A Critical Review" examines the challenges higher education institutions face when transitioning from conventional to online teaching models. Focusing on Ho Chi Minh City Open University (HCMCOU) as it prepares to launch online programs, the study addresses a lack of scholarly literature regarding teacher e-readiness within the Vietnamese context. Through a qualitative critical literature review of empirical studies, the authors synthesized several critical factors into a conceptual framework consisting of five elements: attitudes, technology competency, pedagogy, training, and time constraints.

The findings indicate that while teachers generally hold positive perceptions of e-learning, institutional pressures can cause resistance. Technology competency, specifically familiarity with ICT tools and learning management systems, is vital to readiness. Furthermore, successful online teaching requires a pedagogical shift from teacher-centered models to student-centered approaches. While training is necessary, many existing programs focus too heavily on basic ICT skills and fail to address the pedagogical aspects of online instruction. Additionally, time constraints act as an impediment as faculty struggle to balance course development with existing workloads.

The authors conclude that teacher e-readiness is a multi-dimensional construct requiring psychological, technical, and pedagogical readiness. For institutions like HCMCOU, administrators should implement strategic plans that assess faculty attitudes and skill levels and provide professional development that includes specialized pedagogical training for online environments.

In the study "New Media Usage and Its Perceived Effects on Classroom Communication and Learning Behavior," Patricia Ann E. Vera examines the gap between technologically familiar students and professors who often rely on traditional instructional methods. Conducted at Assumption College in the Philippines with 97 students and 22 professors, the quantitative research utilized structured questionnaires to measure the frequency of use for 13 new media tools and their relationship to student learning behaviors, including technological competence, self-efficacy, and motivation.

Findings indicate that students most frequently use mobile devices, social networking sites, and video-sharing sites, while QR codes and mashups are the least utilized. A perceptual discrepancy exists: students believe professors do not use new media tools as frequently as necessary, while professors perceive students to be highly active on mobile and social platforms. While students reported high levels of technological competence, motivation, and self-efficacy, the study found no direct relationship between new media usage and student self-efficacy or motivation. However, a strong positive correlation was found between technological competence and self-efficacy, and a moderate correlation was found between motivation and self-efficacy.

The study concludes that technology adoption remains superficial, often used for entertainment rather than deep academic engagement. To bridge the communication gap, the research recommends that institutions provide targeted instructional technology training and invest in both infrastructure and the redesign of pedagogical skill sets.

The study "Simulation-Based Instructional Materials on Central Dogma of Molecular Biology" by Cano, Olvis, Disca, and Docena addresses the difficulty of teaching DNA replication, transcription, and translation. Because these molecular processes cannot be directly observed, they are often poorly mastered. Motivated by the shift toward technology-based learning during the COVID-19 pandemic, researchers examined the effectiveness of simulation-based materials on the learning performance and attitudes of Grade 12 STEM learners. Using a mixed-method design, the study integrated digital tools such as LabXchange®, PhET®, DNA Interactive, and Holt’s Central Dogma simulations.

The findings revealed a significant improvement in student performance. Pretest results showed learners were generally "approaching proficiency" with a mean score of 57.55%. Following the intervention, posttest mean scores rose to 83.59%, placing learners in the "advanced" category. Paired-samples t-tests confirmed that score increases for DNA replication, transcription, and translation were all statistically significant (p < 0.05).

Qualitatively, thematic analysis showed students were "Engaged in Experiential Learning." The visual and interactive nature of the simulations allowed students to move beyond imagination to "experiencing" biological processes, helping them understand complex concepts and encouraging evaluative thinking. The study concludes that simulation-based materials are highly effective at bridging the gap between abstract theory and conceptual understanding by providing a safe, interactive, and visual environment for grasping molecular-level mechanisms.

The article "Talk to Them not at Them: A Teacher-Initiated Model of Engagement (TIME) in Online Learning" addresses high attrition rates in online education caused by student isolation and limited teacher-student interaction. This issue is particularly significant for part-time and external students balancing various responsibilities. To combat this, the author proposed the Teacher-Initiated Model of Engagement (TIME), grounded in Holmberg’s Theory of Interaction and Communication. The model emphasizes "guided didactic conversation" through eight techniques, including output affirmation, active listening, quick responses, deadline alerts, clear instructions, the use of emoticons to encourage conversation, maintaining a conducive ICT environment, and providing coaching via online meeting platforms.

Using a quasi-experimental design, the study tracked submission bins in the MOODLE Learning Management System for a course at the University of the Philippines Open University. Results were compared against student performance from the previous three academic years when the TIME model was not used. Findings indicate that implementing TIME significantly improved completion rates. For the first assignment, completion rose from less than 10% to 88.24%. While subsequent assignments showed varying rates, the overall course completion rate was 60%, whereas it would have been only 38% without TIME interventions and flexible deadlines. The study concludes that responsive teachers who "talk to" students through a personal tone and timely feedback can mitigate isolation and improve student retention.

The study "Creating Virtual Corridors: Social Network Discovery and Landscape Patch Connectivity of Permaculture Projects and Initiatives on Facebook" examines the connection between social media discourse and real-world ecological impacts. The researchers introduce the concept of "virtual corridors" to describe intangible digital links that facilitate the movement of permaculture knowledge, technology, and energy between individuals. This research suggests that social relationships in digital spaces can act as precursors to physical landscape management.

Focusing on the Philippines, the researchers identified potential network nodes by analyzing Facebook friends of a focal node. From 1,267 friends, 286 were identified as potential practitioners based on their membership in eighteen Facebook groups related to agriculture and food. To measure connection strength, the researchers developed a Percentage Linkage Strength (%LS) metric, combining a Social Score based on online interactions with a Permaculture Score accounting for offline activities like formal training and projects.

The findings revealed that 14 nodes met the criteria for "virtual corridors," with ten respondents identified as highly significant virtual corridors possessing a %LS of 90% or higher. These top ten individuals, including organic farmers and urban gardeners, were characterized by high online activity and tangible offline commitment. NetLogo simulations predicted that the spread of permaculture information would increase significantly over a two-year period. The researchers concluded that online social networks serve as a functional equivalent to spatial networks, connecting individual landscape patches through shared values and practices.

The article "Reflection on Learner Support Services and Scope of Web-based Services under Distance Education: A Case Study" examines the role of Learner Support Services (LSS) in the success of Open and Distance Learning (ODL) programs. Focusing on the Post Graduate Diploma in Food Safety and Quality Management at Indira Gandhi National Open University, the study surveyed 112 learners to analyze demographic profiles, service usage, and awareness of web-based services.

Findings indicate that LSS is vital for program completion. Successful learners utilized support services at a higher rate (72.97%) than those who did not complete the program (62.69%). Common services included assignment submission and study material availability, peer interaction, and assignment feedback, while 71.67% of learners attended face-to-face counseling for content clarification and motivation.

Regarding digital services, 57% of learners were aware of web-based LSS, and 56.67% of those aware utilized them. Perceptions were positive, with 89.80% believing these services aid timely completion and 94% finding online materials helpful. Most learners used smartphones, laptops, or desktops, with laptops being the most preferred device. Furthermore, 49% of learners expressed a willingness to pay an additional fee, averaging approximately 29.32%, for enhanced web-based LSS. The authors recommend an integrated model combining conventional approaches with digital tools like virtual classes and smartphone-compatible applications.

The application of Augmented Reality (AR) in nursing education offers significant potential for interactive learning, yet a gap exists between development in wealthy nations and implementation in developing regions like the ASEAN area. In countries such as the Philippines and Thailand, budget constraints hinder the adoption of high-tech medical simulations. This exploratory study sought to address this by reviewing existing AR initiatives, identifying affordable development tools, and creating an AR prototype containing Open Educational Resources (OER) for English nursing communication.

The researchers developed a "talking comic strip" prototype using CraftAR, a tool selected for its free license and drag-and-drop interface suitable for non-programmers. The prototype integrated nursing-written scripts, illustrated comic strips, and recorded audio. Evaluation via a usability survey yielded an average System Usability Scale (SUS) score of 68.5937, which exceeds the global mean of 68, indicating relative usability. Students responded favorably, providing high average ratings for the material being better than printed media alone, the enhancement of their learning experience, and the recommendation of the material to training institutions.

The study concludes that AR is accessible to budget-constrained implementers in developing ASEAN countries through free, user-friendly tools. The research suggests that the digital divide in nursing education can be bridged using OER and accessible authoring tools. Future studies should evaluate new AR tools and focus on improving usability, sustainability, and accessibility.

Tuyen Nguyen Chau Bich investigates the challenges of teaching English listening and speaking skills within the e-learning system at Ho Chi Minh Open University (HOU). While the e-learning model offers flexibility and success in subjects like Economics and Finance, it remains ineffective for oral and aural skills due to the communicative needs of English majors, technological limitations, and cultural preferences for traditional instruction.

Using a qualitative methodology, the study surveyed 104 sophomore English majors to examine their perspectives on online versus face-to-face models. The findings reveal that while learners are highly motivated, they strongly prefer hybrid elements. Specifically, 76.92% of respondents believe the system should incorporate face-to-face speaking classes, and 71.15% agree these classes provide greater benefits. Learners perceive in-person interaction as essential for improving pronunciation, fluency, and listening skills across accents, noting that physical classrooms build confidence, facilitate self-correction, and foster better teacher-student relationships.

Learners identified three areas for innovation: increasing face-to-face hours for listening and speaking, implementing structured online listening exercises that progress from simple to complicated, and maintaining consistent teacher-student contact. The study concludes that technology cannot entirely replace the communicative benefits of face-to-face interaction. The author recommends that HOU adopt an integrated approach by increasing contact hours, designing tiered online exercises, and ensuring maintained teacher-learner relationships to improve training quality.

The study "Social Presence among Distance Learners: Portrait of Online Communication at Universitas Terbuka" investigates student isolation in Indonesian distance education, where the self-learning nature of the curriculum may conflict with social cultural needs. The research examines how social presence—the feeling of proximity and intimacy in digital spaces—manifests within the online services of Universitas Terbuka (UT). Using qualitative discourse analysis, the researcher examined interactions in academic online tutorials and non-academic Community Forums, supplemented by focus group discussions and tutor interviews.

Findings reveal a significant difference between these environments. In academic online tutorials, social presence is minimal, characterized by formal language and a strict focus on subject matter. While students use emoticons and profile pictures, "chattering about small things" and sharing personal stories are nearly non-existent. In contrast, social presence is much higher in the non-academic Community Forum, where communication is relaxed and informal. This forum serves as a vital space for students to share experiences, motivate one another, and extend social connections to platforms like WhatsApp or Facebook.

While the forum facilitates student-to-student interaction, institutional responsiveness remains minimal. Working students reported feeling alone due to low response rates from tutors and authorities, while tutors cited busy schedules as a barrier to interaction. The study recommends integrating social presence training into tutor guidance and increasing participation from academic advisors and faculty leadership in forums to mitigate isolation.

In the study "Developing a Multimedia Courseware Using Cognitive Load Theory," Sheila R. Bonito addresses the challenges of nursing education in distance learning, specifically the difficulty of mastering complex clinical skills without physical preceptors. The research utilizes Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) to manage the mental effort required during clinical practicums by addressing intrinsic, extraneous, and germane loads.

The methodology involved a multi-stage approach: interviewing content experts to identify competencies, holding roundtable discussions with specialists to reduce extraneous load, and conducting a pilot review with ten students. The resulting four-step development process focused on selecting necessary tasks, simplifying complexity, reducing extraneous load, and refocusing learners on subject matter.

To manage intrinsic load, the courseware used learning scaffolds like sequencing sub-tasks from simple to complex. Extraneous load was reduced by mimicking a real hospital setting with minimal distracting interactivity and "chunking" case studies into short video clips. Germane load was enhanced through short lessons, self-assessment questions, and glossary hyperlinks. Pilot reviews indicated positive student responses regarding relevance and presentation, though students suggested improvements for navigation and the addition of a tutorial guide. The study concludes that CLT is an effective guide for developing multimedia courseware for complex learning, suggesting that designers should focus on the learner's cognitive architecture.

The study "Evaluating the Use and Acceptance of eLearning for Tertiary Education among Senior High School Students" by Patricia O. Calora and Yrelle Mae R. Lleva examines eLearning and Open and Distance eLearning (ODeL) as solutions to resource challenges in Philippine higher education. Using a quantitative design grounded in the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2), researchers surveyed 200 senior high school students across five K-12 strands to assess their perceptions and intentions regarding online undergraduate studies.

Findings indicate that 71.2% of respondents intend to enroll in an online institution. Most participants were 17-year-old females who use smartphones to access the internet. While students perceive eLearning as flexible and affordable, they lack specific knowledge regarding the practical mechanics of online assessments and virtual collaboration.

Analysis of UTAUT constructs showed that performance expectancy was the only significant predictor of behavioral intention; students more likely to pursue online education were those who believed eLearning would help them achieve academic goals. Other factors, such as effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, hedonic motivation, price value, and habit, were not significant predictors. The authors conclude that intention is driven by perceived utility for academic success. They recommend that institutions implement communication campaigns to explain online system functions and suggest that developers prioritize resource accessibility, student support, and interactive environments.

In "Role of Teachers in Technology-mediated Distance Education: A Preliminary Synthesis," Deeksha Dave examines how technological advancements have shifted educator responsibilities from traditional correspondence models to interactive digital platforms. This evolution from postal services to digital tools like blogs and social media has changed the learner profile, as students now seek flexibility and real-time collaboration. Because students have instant access to online resources, teachers can no longer function merely as dispensers of information.

Using a review-based approach of 50 research papers and primary data from interactions with teachers at various universities, the study identifies several emerging roles for educators. Instead of being the sole authority, teachers become team members, team coordinators, and partners in learning who participate in knowledge exchange. Other roles include trainers, technology-savvy mentors, content developers, and instructional designers.

However, significant challenges hinder implementation, including resource shortages, inadequate staff training, and a lack of expertise in course design. There is a notable gap between the availability of technology and its pedagogical application, as many teachers are trained to operate tools rather than use them specifically for teaching. The paper concludes that successful technology-mediated distance education requires effective faculty participation and a fundamental shift in how instructors view their relationship with students. Institutions must prioritize professional development that focuses on the intersection of technology and pedagogy to empower teachers as guides and collaborators.

In the study "Aggregating Attention, Emotion, and Cognition Load as Basis for Developing a Rule-based Pedagogy for Online Learner," Anna Liza A. Ramos and Melvin A. Ballera address the challenges of maintaining engagement and optimizing outcomes in virtual learning environments. The researchers identify that learners often face distractions, negative emotions like anxiety or frustration, and high cognitive load due to poorly designed instructional materials. While attention, emotion, and cognition have been studied individually, the authors note a gap in using technology, such as electroencephalogram (EEG) signals, to integrate these three components into a cohesive pedagogical framework.

Using a quantitative experimental design, the researchers utilized an Emotiv EPOC+14 Channel Mobile Encephalogram (EEG) tool to record the brain signals of 20 respondents with backgrounds in C++ programming. Participants performed tasks involving reading e-learning materials and completing machine problem activities, generating 5,400 datasets. The researchers used MATLAB EEG tools and various algorithms, including Bandpass filters, Infinite Impulse Response (IIR) filters, Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and Independent Component Analysis (ICA), to process signals and remove noise. The final values for attention load (Al), emotion load (EL), and cognitive load (CL) were aggregated using weighted means and used in a regression model to predict performance scores.

The findings established a mapping system where expert judgment was used to prioritize pedagogies based on simulated analysis and signal classification. The study developed specific criteria for different load levels across all three domains. The simulation demonstrated that the combined values of attention, emotion, and cognition are significant predictors of the learning process. The authors suggest that this rule-based pedagogy offers insights for selecting appropriate learning strategies, moving e-learning toward more individualized, adaptive environments through real-time, data-driven assessments.

The study "Reflective Writing of New Graduate Students: Their Challenges and Experiences in an Open and Distance Education" by Queenie R. Ridulme and Rachel Anne Joyce C. Sales investigates the transition of first-year graduate nursing students into an open and distance learning (ODL) environment at an open university in the Philippines. Using a qualitative research design guided by Gibbs’ Reflective Cycle, the researchers collected data from 13 graduate nursing students via an online self-administered questionnaire.

The findings revealed a dichotomy of experiences. On the positive side, students valued the flexibility of studying at their own pace and from their workplaces, which fostered independence and responsibility. Many participants noted the ability to apply theoretical knowledge to their actual clinical practice, while support from professors and peers and the satisfaction of achieving high grades served as significant motivators.

Conversely, the study identified significant challenges. The most prominent issue was delayed feedback, which caused confusion and tension. Technical difficulties, including poor internet connectivity, power interruptions, and software errors, also emerged as major barriers. Furthermore, students struggled with time management while balancing work, social life, and academic responsibilities.

The authors recommend that instructors provide more frequent and timely feedback and establish clear guidelines for response times. They also advocate for the continuous enhancement of learning tools, regular updating of modules, and ongoing training for faculty in educational technology.
32:
Bioinformatics is a multidisciplinary field merging biology with computer science, mathematics, statistics, and physics. Because it relies on information technology rather than physical laboratories, it is well-suited for Open and Distance Learning (ODL). However, creating ODL bioinformatics curricula is difficult due to the time required for content creation and the rapid evolution of the field. While many free software tools and Integrated Bioinformatics Platforms (IBPs) exist, educators lack established criteria to determine which tools are suitable for distance learners.

To address this, researchers developed an evaluation method to identify software that can be integrated into ODL programs. In September 2016, they evaluated over 40 tools and IBPs, focusing on those cited in research, the Expasy portal, and plant genomic analysis tools. The evaluation used two categories: Usability (including understandability, documentation, learnability, installability, copyright/licensing, and community) and Maintainability (including supportability, evolvability, interoperability, and portability).

Findings showed a diverse usability landscape. While most tools indicated primary functions, only 60% provided comprehensive manuals, 44% included screenshots, and 15% offered audio-visual tutorials. Regarding maintainability, over 75% provided routine updates and platform compatibility, and more than 80% met criteria for evolvability and portability. The study concludes that integrating high-quality existing software is an effective strategy for ODL. Tools scoring higher than six can be integrated directly, while lower-scoring tools require additional instructional support.

Juliet Aleta R. Villanueva’s study, "Teaching Presence in K-12 Blended Learning Classes under the Alternative Delivery Mode," investigates how teaching presence manifests within the Philippine K-12 system's Alternative Delivery Mode (ADM). Using an exploratory case study design, the researcher examined three blended learning classes from three urban public schools through interviews, focus group discussions, observations, and data from Learning Management Systems and Facebook Messenger. The study applied the Community of Inquiry (CoI) model, categorizing teaching presence into design and organization, facilitating discourse, and direct instruction.

The findings demonstrate that teaching presence is strongly manifested and contributes significantly to building learning communities. Teachers showed strength in design and organization by providing clear instructions and goals, and they effectively facilitated discourse using technology like Facebook Messenger. Notably, the study revealed that teaching presence is not exclusive to instructors; students exhibited "peer-facilitation" during collaborative tasks, suggesting a dynamic interaction between teaching presence and cognitive presence.

Despite these strengths, students reported challenges regarding the timeliness of feedback and communication issues caused by technical difficulties or platform bugs. Some students also perceived a lack of presence in teachers who lacked proficiency with educational technology. The researcher proposes a modified CoI framework for K-12 that adds a "Self-direction" category and suggests a "CoI Self-Reflection Tool for Teachers" to help educators become active members of a learning community.

The article "Exploring the Potential of a Ticketing-Based Student Support System for Open and Distance e-Learning Institutions" investigates how automated ticketing systems can enhance quality assurance in student support services within Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL) environments. Because face-to-face interaction is limited in ODeL settings, reliable and timely support is vital for student retention and success.

At the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) within the Bachelor of Arts in Multimedia Studies (BAMS) program, students previously relied on at least eight different formal and informal online sources for information. This fragmentation leads to confusion and the risk of following outdated information. Institutional challenges identified include inconsistent response times, difficulties in record-keeping, loss of information during staff turnover, and the difficulty of providing personalized support to a diverse online student body.

Using a qualitative methodology, the researchers conducted a literature review and performed stakeholder interviews with BAMS students, alumni, and support staff. Findings indicate that ticketing-based systems offer significant benefits, such as improved workflows through automation, 24/7 access to a knowledge base, and data analytics insights. The implementation of Freshdesk in the BAMS program showed positive results by providing a centralized knowledge base that allows students to find solutions via articles before filing a ticket. This ensures information is accurate and up-to-date, while the ticketing feature ensures queries are tracked until resolution.

The authors conclude that ticketing-based systems are a promising intervention to improve support quality by making processes more efficient and responsive. They recommend that ODeL institutions adopt such systems as part of quality assurance frameworks, prioritizing ease of use and staff training. Institutions should also inform students of correct support channels to prevent the use of informal ones.

The study "Use of Tracer Studies to Enhance the UPOU Environment and Natural Resources Management Graduate Program" by Consuelo Dl. Habito and Maripres U. Sarinas evaluates the effectiveness of the Diploma and Master of Environment and Natural Resources Management (MENRM) program at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU). Using a mixed-methods approach, the researchers analyzed admission data from 534 applicants and conducted an online tracer study with 29 graduates from school years 2010-2014.

Applicant profiles showed that 91% were employed, with 48% in private institutions and 34% in government offices. Primary motivations for enrollment included the desire to enhance knowledge and skills, the flexibility of the ODeL format, and the program's relevance to current employment.

The tracer study revealed significant professional benefits. A majority of respondents (52%) experienced job changes during their studies, 62% reported a change in professional rank, 41% were promoted, and 55% reported higher salaries. The program successfully enhanced academic knowledge (79%), confidence in independent learning (72%), critical thinking (65%), research skills (62%), and learning efficiency (62%). Graduates also reported growth in technical responsibility (75%), people management (60%), and policy-making roles (55%).

However, only 38% of graduates felt the program "very much" improved their communication skills. The authors conclude that while the program successfully builds capacity and catalyzes career advancement, the curriculum should strengthen its focus on environmental communication to better prepare graduates to influence public perception and policy.

In "Smart Lecture Video Production: A Case Study with Philosophy and Media Literacy," Tomotsugu Kondo describes how The Open University of Japan (OUJ) developed eight online courses in one year despite limited budgets, tight deadlines, and a lack of professional video crews. The project aimed to produce broadcast-quality content using non-professional staff by implementing a mission-driven philosophy focused on learners, lecturers, and staff.

To support learners, the institution prioritized accessibility by implementing strict audio loudness standards and a custom closed caption function for the Moodle video player. For lecturers, the project utilized renovated warehouse studios and a custom PowerPoint macro-based prompter tool that synchronized scripts with slide transitions to ensure fluent delivery. To assist staff, the author developed a "Script Sheet Generating Tool" using PowerPoint macros, which automatically generated production scripts and time predictions from presentation notes. Technical staff were further supported through video manuals and a television lecture series.

The project was successful, launching the courses in April 2016 and attracting over 4,000 students in the first semester. The methodology allowed for various video formats, including on-location interviews and hand-drawn explanations, with much of the production completed in-house. Kondo concludes that while technical skills are necessary, success depends on a shared philosophy and trust between lecturers and staff. Institutions can overcome resource constraints by investing in custom-built digital tools and a clear organizational mission.

The study "Perceptions of Students to Open and Distance Learning of Review Classes in a Review Center in the Philippines" by Aaron Bryan A. Lopez investigates student perceptions of a pilot distance education program at the Review for Global Opportunities (RGO) Review Center. The research focuses on the psychometrician review program, which transitioned to a home-based, online format in 2018 to accommodate students facing geographical or time constraints. The RGO Review Center utilized print-based materials and online delivery via Facebook, including live and recorded video lectures, review notes, mock examinations, and answer keys.

Findings indicated that respondents were predominantly female and aged 20–29. The primary motivation for choosing distance education was flexibility of time and location (69.6%), followed by work commitments (52.2%) and family commitments (34.8%). Regarding teaching, students generally agreed that the instructional medium was relevant and content met expectations, though feedback on examinations often arrived months after completion. Most students found learning materials self-explanatory, though some experienced workload congestion due to a lack of structured study schedules.

The study concludes that converting offline materials to online formats is insufficient for success. A comprehensive systems approach is required, including structured scheduling, interactive elements, and robust support services. Recommendations include establishing weekly learning schedules, providing prompt feedback through self-grading assessments, facilitating formal asynchronous group discussions, and providing clearer support regarding registration and the transition to home-based modes.
38:
In the concept paper "Using Facebook Metrics to Measure Student Engagement in Moodle," Leonardo Magno addresses the difficulty of accurately measuring student engagement within virtual learning environments. While learning management systems like Moodle provide data logs, these tools often focus on usage rather than the depth of interaction. Magno identifies a research gap regarding the application of social media engagement formulas, specifically Facebook’s engagement rate, to data generated within a learning management system.

The author proposes a modified Moodle Post Engagement Rate (MPER) formula: MPER = (CL + C + L) / R. In this adaptation, "Shares" are removed because course content is typically restricted to class members. "Clicks" (CL) represent post visits, "Comments" (C) represent replies, and "Likes" (L) represent student approval. The "Reach" (R) is defined as the unique number of students who actually viewed the specific forum post.

In a simulation using dummy data, Post A reached 10 students but saw heavy interaction, resulting in an engagement rate of 7%. Post B reached all 30 students but saw minimal interaction, resulting in an engagement rate of 1%. The results suggest the MPER formula successfully identifies Post A as more engaging despite its lower reach. The paper concludes that aggregating data using social media formulas can help instructors understand the qualitative impact of their content and identify effective discussion prompts.

In the article "Developing Facebook as an Accessible and Inclusive Online Personal Learning Platform: Ubiquity is Key," Hannah Kimberly I. Obar addresses the digital divide in the Philippines, specifically regarding the accessibility of Online Personal Learning (OPL) platforms. While Learning Management Systems (LMS) like Moodle and Blackboard facilitate modern learning, they are often inaccessible in the Philippines due to high costs, connectivity issues, and device storage constraints. This leaves marginalized communities and differently-abled learners at a disadvantage.

Using qualitative research methods based on personal observations and the management of 21 Facebook Groups used as makeshift LMS platforms since 2015, the author identifies a gap between sophisticated LMS tools and actual accessibility for the average Filipino learner. The findings reveal that while traditional LMS platforms offer advanced tracking tools, students engage more quickly via Facebook Groups because the application is already installed and the interface is familiar. Facebook Messenger also proved more efficient for communication than traditional discussion forums.

The author proposes "Facebook Classroom," a specialized mode within Facebook that incorporates essential LMS features like gradebooks, assignment bins, and test administration. This proposed platform would include specific modes to assist learners with visual, hearing, navigation, or overstimulation issues. The study suggests that multi-sectoral collaboration is needed to provide discounted data access for this platform, leveraging Facebook's ubiquity to bridge the digital divide.
40:
Queenie Roxas-Ridulme’s study investigates computer self-efficacy (CSE) and attitudes toward e-learning among 33 Master of Arts in Nursing (MAN) students at the University of the Philippines Open University. Using an online survey, the research analyzed how these students perceive their computer abilities and their views on online learning environments.

The findings indicate that students possess high computer self-efficacy at a "beginning" level, though they rated "fairly" in the "advanced" category. While confident in basic tasks like moving a cursor, they showed lower confidence in complex tasks such as troubleshooting hardware or software. Additionally, these students do not extensively use the Internet for educational research, potentially because they are in a non-computer-related discipline.

Regarding attitudes, students demonstrated a highly positive view of e-learning, yielding a total mean score of 4.01. They perceive e-learning as a useful, efficient, and flexible tool for continuing education that facilitates communication and offers equal opportunities for different personality types.

Statistical analysis revealed no significant relationship between computer self-efficacy and attitudes toward e-learning (p-value = 0.902), suggesting that a positive attitude does not depend on a student's level of computer confidence. The researcher recommends encouraging students to use academic databases more extensively and suggests implementing e-counselling to support students facing study difficulties.

The COVID-19 pandemic necessitated a global shift from face-to-face instruction to online learning, requiring students to adapt to self-directed environments. In this context, self-regulation (SR)—the ability to initiate and monitor one's own learning—and online learning self-efficacy (OLSE)—the belief in one's ability to succeed in online tasks—became critical for academic success. This study utilized an analytical-correlational research design to examine the association between these two constructs among nursing students, a group particularly vulnerable to academic stressors.

Using respondent-driven sampling, researchers surveyed 166 nursing students in Pampanga, Philippines, aged 18 to 50. Data were collected via the Online Learning Self-Efficacy Scale (OLSES) and the Short Self-Regulation Questionnaire (SSRQ), then analyzed using descriptive statistics and the Pearson correlation coefficient. Findings revealed that students possess moderate levels of both self-regulation (x = 54.75; SD = 10.60) and online learning self-efficacy (x = 93.01; SD = 25.03). Statistical analysis demonstrated a significant and strong positive association between SR and OLSE (r = .60; p < .001), indicating that increased self-regulation correlates with higher confidence in online learning success.

The researchers concluded that these psychological constructs are interconnected, as self-regulated learners are better equipped to navigate the demands of digital education. The study recommends that educators develop interventions to enhance both skills and suggests that future research explore these dynamics across different regions and academic programs.

Wawasan Open University (WOU) faced financial pressure due to the high costs and long timelines associated with its traditional "wrap-around" course development model. This method relied on expensive textbooks, external writers, graphic designers, and editors, often requiring 12 to 18 months to complete a single course. To address this, the School of Business and Administration investigated integrating Open Educational Resources (OER)—materials available at zero cost under open licenses or in the public domain—to reduce costs and improve accessibility.

Using a descriptive case study of a Microeconomics course, the study compared the traditional model against a revised model utilizing OER. The traditional model incurred costs totaling RM97,103 over four semesters, driven by external writer fees, textbook purchases, and licensing fees. In contrast, the OER model drastically reduced expenses by using full-time academic staff instead of external writers and eliminating textbook and licensing fees. The total cost for the Microeconomics course revision dropped to RM6,987.50, with a "real" cost to the university of approximately RM2,000 when accounting for internal academic time. This transition resulted in total savings of approximately RM1.4 million by mid-2016.

The study concludes that OER supports the mission of keeping tuition fees low and education accessible. However, OER introduces challenges regarding quality assurance. The author suggests the need for a standardized quality assurance framework and recommends future research into OER sustainability and its impact on student learning.

In the article "Group Flow States of Intergenerational Networks Within Age-Friendly Academic Settings," Alexander G. Flor examines how academic institutions maintain vitality during generational transitions. Using the Faculty of Information and Communication Studies at the University of the Philippines Open University as a case study, the research addresses potential systemic dysfunction caused by age and ideological gaps during leadership successions. The institution is considered age-friendly because it encourages the continued involvement of retirement-age faculty, creating a diverse demographic structure.

The author develops a theoretical framework integrating autopoietic theory, systems theory, and flow theory. The study explores "group flow" or "communitas," defined as collective joy shared during common experiences. Through qualitative observations of academic discussions, the research identifies specific triggers for these states, including subject novelty, a collegial atmosphere that suspends rigid social orders, and high levels of communication skills.

Findings indicate that group flow is facilitated by mutual respect for intergenerational expertise, where younger members provide technological authority and older members provide social impact expertise. During these episodes, participants experience effortless creativity and a distorted sense of time. The author concludes that these flow states diminish generational chasms and serve as indicators of autopoietic progression. Fostering environments conducive to group flow can mitigate systemic dysfunction and leverage intergenerational networks to drive continuous organizational evolution.

In the article "Special Report on Technology Application Design and Development of an Online Repository System for Thesis and Special Problem Manuscripts," Armacheska R. Mesa addresses challenges at the University of the Philippines (UP) Mindanao regarding the management of scholarly intellectual output. Existing manual storage methods, involving physical copies and optical discs, pose risks of loss, misplacement, and media degradation, which can lead to research works becoming obscured.

To resolve these issues, the author developed the UP Mindanao Manuscript e-library and Repository System (UPMERS). This web-based system provides a centralized digital archive for teachers, students, researchers, and alumni to search and retrieve titles, abstracts, and full manuscripts. It includes features to ensure compliance with Intellectual Property Rights by allowing administrators to restrict content access. Developed using the Rapid Application Development (RAD) framework, the system was built with PHP, MySQL, HTML, CSS, and Javascript.

Evaluation through black-box testing and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) showed that UPMERS successfully enables faster record retrieval and secure storage. The system achieved a System Usability Scale score of 85.5, indicating it is user-friendly. Furthermore, users reported high perceived usefulness in monitoring research and eliminating duplication. The author concludes that UPMERS is an effective tool but notes that future success depends on populating the database through departmental requirements.

The study "Ask Iska and IskOU: Analysis of UPOU's Chatbot for Information Support Services" investigates the performance and user satisfaction of two AI chatbots, Iska and IskOU, developed by the University of the Philippines Open University. These tools aim to streamline information support for students, faculty, and the public via Facebook and the university website. Using a mixed-methods approach, researchers collected data from forty-one respondents and evaluated the chatbots based on response time, multi-thread conversation, maxim of quantity, perceived ease of use, and the recognition of user goals and intent.

Findings regarding performance were mixed. The chatbots performed exceptionally well in response time, with 100% of respondents reporting prompt answers and an average response time of 900 milliseconds. Users found the tools intuitive, reporting high levels of perceived ease of use and usefulness. However, significant limitations were identified regarding the chatbots' ability to interpret intent. While successful at answering frequently asked questions regarding application procedures and program lists, they struggled with complex or highly specific queries. Approximately 24.4% of users reported the chatbot "sometimes" answered completely, while 22% reported it "never" answered completely.

The study concludes that while the chatbots are successful for high-volume, repetitive tasks, they are not yet a complete replacement for human support. Researchers suggest expanding the knowledge base, improving the ability to provide direct answers rather than external links, and implementing monitoring schemes to track unresolved queries.

The study "Pedagogical Purposes of Using Open Educational Resources in STEM Education: A Case Study in a STEM High School in Egypt" by Eiman Yassin and Insung Jung examines how teachers in a developing country utilize Open Educational Resources (OER) to support STEM education. In many developing contexts, implementing effective STEM curricula is hindered by a lack of high-quality instructional materials and the limited capacity of teachers to develop specialized resources. OER, which allows for the reuse, remixing, and redistribution of resources, offers a cost-effective solution to these shortages.

Using a qualitative case study approach at a STEM boarding school in Egypt, the researchers collected data through semi-structured interviews with six teachers and nine students, classroom observations, and syllabus analysis. The researchers identified four main types of OER used in STEM sessions: PDF references acting as primary online textbooks, videos, educational websites, and online quizzes.

The analysis revealed three primary pedagogical purposes for these resources. First, maintaining motivation accounted for 44% of uses, with teachers using OER to create real-life connections and encourage engagement. Second, seeking information accounted for 40% of uses, helping students learn core content and conduct research. Third, developing student competencies accounted for 16% of uses, helping improve active learning and independent learning skills. The researchers conclude that OER plays a vital role in developing nations, often serving as foundational instructional material that supports 21st-century competencies.
47:
Ricardo T. Bagarinao’s study examines the vulnerability of online learners to natural hazards in the Philippines. While online learning serves as a disaster-resilient response to ensure education continuity, the modality depends heavily on stable electricity and internet connectivity. In a country where hydrometeorological events account for 80% of natural disasters, disruptions to digital infrastructure pose significant threats to academic continuity and student well-being.

Using a descriptive research design and Geographic Information System (GIS), the researcher analyzed the profiles of 3,225 open and distance e-learning (ODeL) students from the 2020–2021 academic year. Student locations were intersected with Manila Observatory disaster risk maps to assess vulnerability to typhoons, extreme rainfall, and earthquakes.

Findings show a significant concentration of students in high-risk areas. Over 80% of learners reside in areas with high to very high risks regarding changes in rainfall patterns, and 83% are in high-risk typhoon zones. Additionally, 65% are in medium-risk earthquake zones and 9% in high-risk earthquake zones. This spatial distribution creates a "double disaster" where students face physical hazards alongside the academic and psychological stress of being unable to participate in learning.

The author suggests institutions develop "offline learning experiences" through downloadable materials and LMS features with offline capabilities. Recommendations include policies to protect copyright during offline use, increased flexibility in teaching and assessment, and mental health support to prevent student disengagement or dropout.

The study "Measuring System Usability and Readiness of System Users for Basic Healthcare Awareness and Education: A Case Study" by Cinmayii A. Garligos-Manliguez examines the inefficiencies of manual healthcare operations in Philippine barangay health centers, such as time-consuming record searches and inconsistent verbal education. To address these issues, the researcher developed eHICAP, an electronic system for the Barangay Sto. Niño Health Center that manages patient records and provides an interactive e-learning module using multimedia content. The system was developed using the Scrum Agile Development Model and open-source technologies.

The research employed the System Usability Scale (SUS), the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and the Test of eLearning Related Attitudes (TeLRA) to evaluate the system. Findings regarding usability were highly positive; eHICAP achieved an average SUS score of 74, exceeding the recommended acceptance rating of 68. Users reported the system was easy to use and believed it would streamline report generation and improve records management. The e-learning module was also viewed as a valuable educational tool.

However, TeLRA results revealed a nuanced view of workforce readiness. While 94.7% of workers agreed e-learning is beneficial, there was only moderate agreement regarding implementation challenges like mental effort. Attitudes toward computer systems were split, potentially due to digital fatigue or an age-related digital divide. The study concludes that technical deployment should be accompanied by human-centric support, such as training.

The study "Open and Distance eLearning Readiness of a State University Graduate Students" by Randy Joy Magno Ventayen and Caren Casama Orlanda investigates the preparedness of graduate students at Pangasinan State University Open University Systems (PSU OUS) to transition from a hybrid model to a fully open and distance eLearning (ODeL) environment. Using a quantitative methodology and purposive sampling, the researchers assessed Master's and Doctorate students across five dimensions: self-direction, learning preferences, study habits, technology skills, and computer equipment capabilities.

The findings indicate that graduate students are ready for ODeL, maintaining a positive attitude with an overall weighted mean of 4.07. Self-direction received the highest mean (4.21), followed by technology skills (4.16), learning preferences (4.13), computer equipment capabilities (3.99), and study habits (3.93). Most respondents were female millennials enrolled in the Master of Arts in Education program who worked as teachers.

Significant correlations were identified between student profiles and readiness. Level of education related to readiness in self-direction and study habits, while passing a licensure examination correlated with readiness in study habits. Additionally, years of teaching experience showed a significant relationship with readiness regarding computer equipment capabilities. The researchers concluded that students are competent for a shifting educational environment, suggesting that the university implement a comprehensive learning management system and that the Department of Education develop long-term technological adaptation strategies.

The study "Analyzing the Role of an Online System in Reducing Learner’s Transactional Time in an Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL) Environment: A Landscape Connectivity Perspective" investigates how the Online Request for Document System (ORDS) at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) impacts administrative efficiency. Using landscape connectivity theory, researchers viewed the distance education environment as a fragmented landscape where learners are physically and functionally separated from the institution. The study aimed to determine if the ORDS reduces the transactional time required for non-academic tasks and to evaluate student satisfaction regarding usefulness, ease of use, and efficiency.

Data from 190 students and an analysis of processing logs revealed a significant reduction in transactional time. The manual system required an average of 14 days to deliver documents, whereas the ORDS reduced this to an average of 4 days. Furthermore, the online system increased request volume, with the Office of the University Registrar processing a monthly average of 149 requests, which was 36% higher than the manual system's volume.

Students reported high satisfaction, with all mean scores exceeding four on a 5-point Likert scale, noting significant savings in time, money, and travel risks. While students requested more payment options and real-time interaction features, the study concludes that the ORDS acts as a "virtual corridor" that enhances connectivity and helps students manage time more effectively, which is vital for academic persistence.

As higher education institutions adopt technology-mediated teaching, the use of Learning Objects (LOs)—short, reusable, digital materials designed for specific objectives—has become an essential approach to establishing standards for digital materials. To support this shift, the Interactive Learning Center at the University of the Philippines Los Baños initiated the development of multimedia LOs for undergraduate programs.

This study assessed a specific LO centered on the "Consumption Function" in Economics to determine its effectiveness as a supplementary resource. Conducted during the 2017-2018 academic year with 134 ECON 11 students, the research employed a pre-test-post-test design comparing a control group receiving regular classroom discussion to a treatment group receiving both discussion and the LO.

Findings revealed that the LO significantly enhanced student knowledge gain. While both groups improved from pre-test to post-test, the treatment group achieved a significantly higher mean post-test score (4.83) than the control group (3.71). Socio-demographic factors had no significant effect on knowledge gain. Quality evaluations were highly positive, with high ratings for clarity and comprehensibility (4.48), applicability (4.40), attractiveness (4.39), interactivity (4.30), and assessment function (4.30). Overall, respondents agreed (4.36) that the LO enhanced their learning. The study supports the integration of multimedia tools in higher education, though researchers recommend refinements to color brightness, graphics, navigation, and question difficulty.

The article "Knowledge Sharing and Co-Creation: the UPOU’s Master of Public Management Program’s Innovation on Quality Assurance for ODeL" examines how the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) utilizes faculty externships to enhance its Master of Public Management (MPM) program. The study addresses the need for continuous quality assurance and content updates in a program designed for government practitioners. A primary challenge identified is that public administration is highly context-based, making academic journals alone insufficient for providing the real-world context required for effective learning.

To bridge the gap between theory and practice, the authors implemented faculty externships, which are short-term experiential learning opportunities where faculty observe programs and local governance practices firsthand. Findings reveal that these externships contribute to quality assurance by facilitating the creation of Open Educational Resources (OERs), such as online video case studies. The strategy also fosters professional development, improves syllabus design, and facilitates partnerships with institutions like the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) and various local government units. Furthermore, the externships serve as a platform for "co-creation," where knowledge is produced through interactions between faculty, local experts, and students. The authors conclude that this model is an effective innovation for Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL), though challenges such as video editing, scheduling, and internet connectivity must be managed.

The study "Analysis of Students’ Reflections and Ideation in an Online Graduate Ecology Course" investigates how teaching approaches utilizing student reflections and ideation can foster environmental advocacy. Addressing the global plastic pollution crisis, the research focused on students in the Master of Environment and Natural Resources Management program at the University of the Philippines Open University. Researchers analyzed 242 student reflection outputs from 2013 to 2017, examining how students applied course concepts to a video regarding the plastic bottled water industry. The methodology employed Potter’s Theory of Media Literacy and categorized responses into cognitive, emotional, and social ideation.

Findings revealed that the online reflective-reflexive approach successfully encouraged critical and creative thinking. Cognitive ideation showed students understood the risks plastics pose to health and ecosystems, while noting the tension between environmental values and poverty-driven "sachet" culture. Social ideation progressed from personal pledges to calls for community-wide changes and challenging corporate interests. Emotional ideation involved feelings of guilt, sadness, anger, and empathy for wildlife. Ultimately, students began viewing themselves as active contributors to solutions.

The study concludes that graduate ecology students require dedicated spaces for reflexivity to translate scientific knowledge into action. Researchers found audio-visual materials more effective than print for multi-sensory learning and noted that online environments facilitate deep engagement. The authors recommend integrating sociology and psychology into environmental education to help students demystify corporate media messages through a "bottom-up" approach.

In "The Promotion of ASEAN Regional Integration Through Open and Distance Higher Education," Alexander G. Flor explores how Open, Distance, and eLearning (ODeL) can serve as a strategic tool to achieve the goals of the ASEAN Economic Community (AEC). The study addresses the need for a collective human resource development strategy and the "absorptive capacity" problem, noting that higher education infrastructure has not kept pace with projected student growth. While developed nations use ODeL to enhance research, developing nations require it to solve issues of scale, access, and equity.

Using a scoping study approach, the research framework treats the integration of ODeL into ASEAN higher education as an ongoing process influenced by acceptability, accessibility, equity, and quality of outcomes. Findings indicate that policy intervention is required in several areas. There is currently no ASEAN-wide policy for mainstreaming ODeL, and disparities in telecommunications infrastructure persist. Furthermore, focus must remain on targeting marginalized communities for equity, and there is a need for standardized content, pedagogy, and assessment to ensure quality.

The author concludes that ODeL is uniquely suited to promote "ASEAN Connectivity" through physical, institutional, and people-to-people links. Recommendations include developing ODeL programs with "ASEANization" themes, creating an ODeL Consortium to manage content and credit transfers, and utilizing the ASEAN Qualifications Reference Framework for credential harmonization. Finally, the author warns against the commercialization of ODeL, arguing it should be managed as a tool for regional competitiveness.
56:
Felix Librero examines the crisis of predatory publishing and its impact on faculty evaluations within the University of the Philippines (UP) System. The UP System has implemented a policy to exclude articles from predatory journals when evaluating scientific productivity, promotions, or Professor Emeritus titles. This decision risks the professional standing of academics whose research may have been published in such venues.

The rise of predatory publishing is linked to the evolution of open-access models since 2002. These deceptive practices are characterized by weak or non-existent peer review, editorial boards composed of unconsenting individuals, and a lack of authentic addresses. Such journals often engage in aggressive promotion, maintain high acceptance rates, and charge exorbitant fees. Data from Jeffrey Beall shows a geometric increase in this problem; between 2011 and 2015, the number of predatory publishers rose from 18 to 693.

The author notes that predatory publishing is expanding geometrically while academic solutions progress only linearly. Crucially, publication in a predatory journal does not automatically mean the research itself is of low quality. Librero suggests that while excluding these publications is an internal university matter, implementation must be handled with care. He recommends that the UP System avoid retroactive exclusions and instead apply them to future calls for promotions using standards from legitimate organizations like DOAJ or OASPA to avoid ambiguity.

The study "Design of a Virtual Learning Environment Implementation Framework for State Universities in the Philippines: A Case of Mariano Marcos State University" addresses the challenges of transitioning to digital instruction. At Mariano Marcos State University (MMSU), instruction previously relied on face-to-face discussions without a formalized, university-wide Virtual Learning Environment (VLE). Researchers aimed to design a framework to innovate instructional delivery and introduce new pedagogic models.

The methodology involved a multi-faceted assessment of 537 respondents, including 160 faculty members and 377 students. Tools used included an ICT infrastructure assessment rubric, a faculty ICT profile self-evaluation, and the JISC infoNet tool. The researchers also conducted a comparative analysis of seven open-source VLE platforms: Chamilo, Claroline, Dokeos, eFront, ILIAS, Moodle, and Sakai.

Findings revealed moderate ICT infrastructure implementation, with high ratings for software but moderate ratings for computers, networks, and internet connectivity. Faculty ICT skills were rated as intermediate, with specific inadequacies in database use, graphics, information searching, telecommunications, copyright ethics, and video production. Users prioritized access, security, tracking achievements, and archiving capabilities. Moodle was identified as the most suitable VLE for MMSU.

The researchers designed a framework consisting of Users, Environment, VLE Architecture (utilizing Moodle), and Implementation Requirements. Recommendations include implementing faculty development programs, appointing a VLE system administrator, allocating budgets for infrastructure and training, upgrading network bandwidth to Gigabit levels, and resolving interoperability issues.
