The study "Impact of Virtual Reality in Maritime Education and Training: The Case of the Maritime Academy of Asia and the Pacific" investigates the effectiveness of Virtual Reality (VR) compared to traditional teaching methods. Prompted by the 2010 Manila Amendments to the STCW Convention, the research sought to determine if VR could help improve seafarer quality to meet global standards.

The researchers conducted a case study involving first-year Bachelor of Science Marine Transportation students. An experimental design compared a VR-based teaching group (n=19) with a traditional teaching group (n=18) as they studied ME and MC Diesel Engines. Performance was measured through 25-question diagnostic and assessment tests.

Findings revealed that VR-based teaching significantly outperformed traditional methods. The VR group achieved a mean score of 20.84%, while the traditional group achieved 10.44%. With a p-value of 0.026456, the researchers rejected the null hypothesis, indicating that VR improves the ability to visualize complex machinery and enhances knowledge retention.

Qualitative data showed students valued the realism and immersion, which allowed them to visualize the scale of ship engines. Benefits included easier comprehension, self-paced learning, and increased engagement. While students reported concerns regarding eye strain, headaches, and hardware costs, 91.9% expected to use VR in future education. The study concludes that VR is an effective tool for bridging the gap between theoretical instruction and practical application.

The article "Developing and Evaluating a Website as an OER for Faculty Development" addresses the need for effective faculty development (FD) programs in liberal arts institutions. In East Asia, new faculty trained at large research universities often struggle to adapt to the pedagogical requirements of liberal arts education. At the International Christian University (ICU) in Japan, there was an urgent need to support new faculty in understanding liberal arts values, mastering instructional design, and balancing professional responsibilities with well-being.

Using the ADDIE model, researchers developed a web-based FD program consisting of 20 modules categorized into administrative functions (R-Modules), tenure and teaching effectiveness (I-Modules), and liberal arts values and teaching strategies (T-Modules). The website was built using Google Sites and released under a Creative Commons license as an Open Educational Resource (OER).

Evaluation through qualitative and quantitative methods indicated the website is an effective tool. Qualitative analysis showed materials were informative and easy to navigate, though participants requested a Japanese version. Quantitative results showed an average System Usability Scale score of 73, exceeding the global mean of 68. High scores for Perceived Usefulness and Perceived Ease of Use suggest the site is useful and user-friendly. The study concludes that digital OERs can support long-term FD through flexible, self-paced learning and suggests future research include longitudinal studies to track long-term utilization.

The study "Social Media as Communication and Learner Support Tool in Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs)" investigates how digital communication channels support learners within the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) MODeL platform. Addressing the global challenge of high dropout rates in MOOCs, the research examines how specific tools function as learner support mechanisms. Using descriptive content analysis, researchers analyzed inquiries from the MODeL Learning Management System (LMS), Gmail, and a Facebook Page during 2017 and 2018. These inquiries were categorized by theme and classified into administrative, technical, instructional, and counseling and tutorial support.

Findings indicate that students select platforms based on the nature of their inquiries. Facebook was primarily used for administrative matters, with 61.7% of its 2018 inquiries relating to Registration and Enrollment. Email was the preferred medium for Counseling and Tutorial Support, specifically regarding course details, materials, degree programs, and certificates. The LMS was utilized for inquiries concerning results, enrollment, and submission requirements. Counseling and Tutorial Support constituted the largest portion of inquiries at 42%, while administrative inquiries accounted for 30%, instructional for 25%, and technical support for 3%.

The authors conclude that UPOU’s multi-channel approach successfully provides accessible lifelong education. They suggest MOOC providers should optimize support by ensuring channels are adequately staffed for specific inquiry types. Future research should examine the relationship between these support mechanisms and course completion rates.
61:
The study "Students’ Readiness for Online and Distance Education at the Nueva Vizcaya State University" by Micah Ryan B. Ramel investigates the preparedness of incoming freshmen for online and distance education (OLDE). This research supports the university's strategic goal to become a premier provider of high-quality Open Distance Education programs and a dual-mode institution. The study focuses on technological competence, self-directed learning abilities, and attitudes toward e-learning.

Using a quantitative research design, the researcher surveyed 38 graduating students in the Accountancy, Business and Management track at the NVSU College of Teacher Education Senior High School. Findings indicate that respondents are generally prepared for OLDE. Students were rated as competent in using offline computer-based, mobile-based, and internet-based technologies. They were also rated as "often" self-directed in their learning and demonstrated favorable attitudes toward e-learning.

Significant positive correlations were found between offline computer-based activities and attitudes toward learning, as well as between mobile internet, internet-based activities, and attitudes toward e-learning. Additionally, a significant positive correlation exists between internet-based activities and self-directed learning and control. However, no significant correlations were found between internet access and self-directed learning, control, or attitudes. The researcher recommends enhancing ICT capability through infrastructure investment, transitioning up to 25 percent of contact hours to online modalities, and adopting a staggered transition to e-learning via a University-wide Learning Management System.
62:
This ethnographic case study investigates how cultural factors influenced student engagement in the "UPOUDC Digital Collective," an online co-creation project at the University of the Philippines Open University. The project aimed to produce open educational resources through student and alumni collaboration but failed to meet production targets due to insufficient sustained interaction and community development. The research suggests this failure stemmed from cultural influences rather than technological limitations.

Data collected from nine participants revealed several key themes, including the importance of camaraderie, hierarchy, and recognition. While initial recruitment was successful due to "utang na loob" (debt of gratitude), long-term engagement was hindered by specific Filipino cultural traits. "Hiya" (shame) caused students to hesitate when sharing ideas for fear of appearing inferior, a behavior linked to "pakikiramdam" (sensing others), where members cautiously "felt out" the group before interacting. Additionally, "ningas cogon" described how initial enthusiasm rapidly diminished. The lack of a defined hierarchy also hindered coordination, as students tended to defer to senior members.

The study concludes that the project remained a "pseudo community" because cultural desires to avoid embarrassment and confrontation prevented the conflict resolution necessary for a true community. To improve future initiatives, the author recommends designing online activities with high cultural consciousness, implementing structured organizational roles, and utilizing recognition systems, such as digital badges, to validate student contributions.
63:
The article "Automated Student Advising: An App for Greater Efficiency" examines logistical challenges in academic advising within the Faculty of Information and Communication Studies (FICS) at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU). In an open and distance e-learning environment, the transition to a one-time enrollment model rendered manual practices, such as face-to-face meetings for nominating advisers, insufficient. The lack of an automated system caused difficulties in record-keeping, managing faculty workloads, and reducing human error during committee designation for the DComm, MDC, and BAMS programs.

To resolve these issues, researchers developed the Online Advisory Committee (AdCom) App using an Iterative Incremental Model. The system features three user categories: Students, Advisers, and Administrators. Students can select committee members based on faculty names, photos, and research specializations, while a "quota" filter ensures equitable faculty workloads. Once a nomination is submitted, the system sends automated emails to faculty for acceptance or declination. Administrators can manage profiles, adjust quotas, and generate the official Nomination and Designation of Dissertation Committee Form.

Findings indicate that the AdCom App successfully enables students to formulate committees online. By displaying research interests, the app helps students make informed decisions to ensure committee members complement their research topics. The system streamlines administrative tasks through automated form generation and provides an efficient method for managing faculty loads. The researchers conclude that the app offers a more convenient, sustainable, and paperless method of student support compared to manual practices.
64:
The sudden shift to online learning during the COVID-19 pandemic forced university instructors in Tokyo to adapt their teaching methods. At Rikkyo University, instructors in English Discussion Classes implemented flipped learning (FL) to address the loss of face-to-face interaction and maximize student speaking time. By moving teacher-fronted instruction to individual learning spaces, instructors aimed to free up class time for interactive, student-centered activities.

Using a reflective research design, four instructors implemented the model over one semester through three stages: preparation, implementation, and reflection. Preparation involved creating instructional videos and pre-lesson tasks, such as pop quizzes and forum discussions, which students completed via a Learning Management System before online sessions.

Findings indicated several benefits, including saved in-class time for student-student interaction and increased student autonomy, as learners could replay videos at their own pace. The model also allowed for differentiated instruction and provided instructors with insights into specific student difficulties through pre-lesson assignments. However, challenges included decreased student motivation, increased workloads for both instructors and students, and difficulties transitioning from passive to active learning styles. Technical issues and communication barriers in virtual spaces also emerged. While limited by a small sample size and reliance on instructor observations, the study suggests flipped learning has significant potential for fostering independent, active learners in mixed-ability classrooms.
65:
In the study "Online Student Engagement and Sense of Community in a Philippine Online University," Al Francis D. Librero investigates the relationship between student engagement and sense of community among Bachelor of Arts in Multimedia Studies students at the University of the Philippines Open University. Using a quantitative approach with the Online Student Engagement (OSE) scale and the Classroom Community Scale (CCS), the researcher surveyed 67 students from introductory and advanced courses to compare perceptions across different residency lengths.

The findings revealed a moderate positive correlation (r = 0.442) between student engagement and sense of community. While students exhibited fair to moderate levels of engagement regarding self-motivation and effort, engagement in interpersonal interactions, such as social chatting, was notably low. Regarding sense of community, students were largely neutral; they felt encouraged to ask questions but did not feel the course was "like a family" and reported a lack of interdependence. No statistically significant difference in engagement or community was found between first-year and third-year students. Notably, almost all respondents reported that the COVID-19 pandemic and natural calamities detrimentally affected engagement due to technical issues, such as poor internet and power failures, as well as mental and emotional stress. The researcher suggests that universities should design online experiences that encourage interaction through platforms like Zoom or Discord and establish student organizations to foster belonging.
66:
In the study "Student support in an open and distance electronic learning (ODeL) context: The experiences of students with disabilities in KwaZulu-Natal," Zwelakhe Erick Cebisa examines inclusivity and equal access in higher education. While ODeL institutions aim for flexibility, a gap exists in understanding the lived experiences of students with disabilities (SWDs). Many SWDs face barriers such as inadequate physical infrastructure, a lack of assistive technologies, and systemic failures in specialized academic support, issues which were exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic's rapid shift to digital platforms.

Using a qualitative, exploratory design within an interpretivism paradigm, the researcher interviewed 10 participants with albinism, physical disabilities, and visual impairments via MS Teams. Thematic analysis revealed several critical findings. Participants reported significant discrimination and a lack of prioritization regarding their needs. Accessibility remains a major hurdle, as computer laboratories are often not disability-friendly and resource constraints lead to a lack of assistive devices or delays in receiving braille and large-print materials. Additionally, students with albinism reported safety concerns due to local myths and a lack of institutional support during transit. While disability forums were noted as a positive, the transition to online learning created inequities, such as the lack of extra time for online examinations.

The study concludes that institutions must move from reactive to proactive support. The author recommends active consultation with SWDs during policy design, developing disability-friendly technology, and implementing change management to ensure online transitions do not strip students of established accommodations.
67:
In the study "Applying the E-learning Framework: Evaluating an E-learning Course toward the Improvement of Quality of ODeL Programs," Myra D. Oruga and Jelaine R. Bagos examine the complexities of evaluating Open and Distance E-learning (ODeL) environments. The researchers applied the "Evaluation Dimension" of Khan’s Eight-Dimensional E-Learning Framework to assess the course IH 213 (Health Promotion for Equity and Sustainable Development) at the University of the Philippines Open University. The study aimed to evaluate the course's relevance to learners, reflective thinking, interactivity, tutor support, peer support, and the interpretation of messages.

Using a survey research design, data were collected from thirty-three international health learners via an online questionnaire. The findings revealed that the e-learning course was perceived as highly effective in most dimensions. Students reported that the content was relevant to professional practice and that they engaged in critical thinking. Furthermore, tutor support, peer support, and the clarity of messages were rated highly.

However, interactivity was identified as a relative weakness, as students reported only "sometimes" asking classmates to explain ideas or responding to their ideas. This suggests that active interaction between learners is lower than other metrics. The authors conclude that while the course is effective in most areas, interactivity requires improvement. They recommend implementing graded discussion forums, incentives for participation, or activities like debates to enhance the quality of the ODeL program.
68:
The study "Online Facilitation of Field Instruction for the Social Work Programs of UP Open University" by Finaflor F. Taylan and Paula Grace Muyco investigates the effectiveness of online facilitation for field instruction (FI) within the Diploma in/Master of Social Work (D/MSW) program at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU). The researchers addressed a gap in research regarding clinical preparation in programs where internships are facilitated online, which is significant for UPOU students who are geographically dispersed.

Using a qualitative design and thematic analysis, the researchers analyzed 12 final sharing outputs from the 2016-2017 academic year. The study utilized Kolb and Fry’s (1974) Experiential Learning Cycle as a theoretical framework. Findings revealed that students successfully navigated all four stages of the cycle. During the concrete experience stage, students provided detailed accounts of agency profiles and activities. In the reflective observation stage, students identified challenges like emotional struggles and managing responsibilities, which led to realizations regarding professional competencies and the application of theory to practice. In the abstract conceptualization stage, students reported gaining technical knowledge and life skills. Finally, in the active experimentation stage, students provided recommendations for agencies and the program.

The authors conclude that online facilitation is effective, as the open and distance e-learning framework allowed students to maximize experiential learning and integrate theory and practice through guided reflection.
69:
The study "A Meta-Interpretation of Collaborative Learning Activities in an R&D Management Online Degree Program" investigates collaborative learning within Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL) environments. Focusing on the Diploma in Research & Development Management at the University of the Philippines Open University, the researchers examined learner experiences through a mini-case study and a WebQuest. Using a meta-interpretive approach, the authors synthesized qualitative research into four themes: purpose, learner experience, teacher’s role, and format.

Regarding purpose, collaboration deepens learning through reflection and broadens perspectives by exchanging diverse professional experiences. While learners found activities enjoyable and socially interactive, they faced challenges such as geographical and time differences, difficulty scheduling meetings, and issues with co-learner responsiveness or missed deadlines. The teacher's role was described as a dual reality; while students valued informal interaction during the collaborative phase, they also highly valued the teacher's active presence as a facilitator who provides feedback and a "personal touch." Regarding format, students required flexibility in topics and resources, alongside clear structures like explicit objectives and well-timed assignments.

The study concludes that successful online collaboration requires a balance of structure and flexibility. To support students, instructors should design activities with specific timing, provide clear guidelines and scaffolding, and incorporate peer assessment to ensure individual accountability and the co-creation of knowledge.
71:
The study "Assessing the Practices for the Conduct of Graduate Students’ Thesis at the Faculty of Management and Development Studies, UP Open University" examines administrative practices for graduate thesis work within an Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL) environment. The research addresses challenges caused by spatial and temporal gaps between students and faculty, which can complicate research supervision. Using a qualitative approach involving content analysis, interviews, and surveys, the researchers examined four Master’s programs: Master of ASEAN Studies, Master of Arts in Nursing, Master of International Health, and Master of Land Valuation and Management.

Findings reveal that the programs implement several ideal practices, such as establishing prerequisites like comprehensive exams and utilizing technology for orientations and communication via email, discussion forums, and social media. Support systems, including library services and monitoring task forces, are also in place. However, significant gaps exist between current practices and student needs. Students reported insufficient guidance, unclear expectations regarding thesis quality, and difficulties adhering to timelines. The "distance-ness" of the programs can magnify issues like scheduling consultation meetings and receiving consistent feedback.

The researchers concluded that while a foundation aligned with ODeL standards exists, implementation is inconsistent. Recommendations include explicitly defining high-quality thesis characteristics, providing advisers with training on online feedback technologies, offering online research skill courses, developing an automated learning management system for advising, and promoting learner interaction to reduce isolation.
72:
Edited by Chib, May, and Barrantes, *Impact of Information Society Research in the Global South* examines how Information and Communication Technologies (ICTs) influence international development. The book seeks to identify concrete evidence regarding the impact of ICTs on socio-economic objectives through practical implementation, policy influence, and media coverage. A primary goal is to promote "homegrown" scholarship by providing a platform for thinkers from Africa, Latin America, and Asia, moving the discourse away from a reliance on scholars from outside the region.

The text is organized into two parts: theoretical discussions regarding measurement lenses and the "research-policy jungle," and empirical case studies in sectors like agriculture and education. Methodologically, the work emphasizes participatory methods that prioritize contextual references and the voices of primary stakeholders.

Findings indicate that while ICT applications are often innovative, they present significant complexities. For example, a mobile-health application in India raised ethical concerns regarding the disclosure of private medical histories to non-physician technicians. Furthermore, researchers face barriers in influencing policy due to academic jargon and a failure to promote work outside scholarly circles. The book concludes that impactful ICTD research must bridge the gap between academia, practice, and policy. It must move beyond theory to establish causation and ensure that the user perspective remains central to the research process to effectively inform real-world development.
74:
Cenie M. Vilela-Malabanan and Nancy Q. Echavez investigated the constraints academics face when using a Learning Management System (LMS) in a blended learning environment at a state university in Mindanao, Philippines. Using a mixed-methods design involving interviews with thirty-three academics and analysis of Moodle computer logs, the study identified four major dimensions of constraints: time management, curriculum level, students' access and economic viability, and students' work and validity of control.

Regarding time management, academics reported that preparing digital materials is more time-consuming than traditional methods, increasing workloads as they manage both physical and online interactions. Curriculum constraints varied by subject; technology-driven courses struggled with laboratory availability, while non-technology courses faced limited student computer access. Additionally, computational subjects were harder to teach effectively online compared to descriptive subjects. Economic factors were a major concern, as students often lack personal computers or reliable internet. This leads to academic anxiety regarding teaching performance and the integrity of unsupervised online assessments.

Quantitative log analysis confirmed that while academics frequently use the LMS for uploading resources, the use of interactive features like forums and chats is significantly lower due to curriculum and economic limitations. The researchers conclude that LMS usage is heavily influenced by the socio-technological landscape, suggesting that administrators must address student technology access, improve infrastructure, and review teaching loads to support digital resource development.
75:
The study "Computer-based Simulation and its Effects on Student’s Knowledge and Interest in Chemistry" by Jhenly I. Asedillas and Maria Ana T. Quimbo investigates how computer-based simulation (CBS) impacts student learning and engagement. Prompted by the difficulty students face in mastering Chemistry, the researchers used a quasi-experimental design to study 143 students from a male boarding school in the Southern Tagalog province. Participants were divided into three homogeneous groups: advanced, proficient, and approaching proficiency. The intervention involved using Physics Education Technology (PhET) interactive simulations to teach chemical reaction concepts over three weeks.

Findings demonstrate that CBS effectively increased knowledge across all three learning groups. The advanced group showed the greatest increase in mean scores (10.980), followed by the proficient group (10.490) and the group approaching proficiency (4.614). Regarding interest, advanced and proficient students reported high interest, while those approaching proficiency reported moderate interest. Qualitative data indicated students enjoyed the simulations due to gamified elements, the ability to manipulate materials independently, the safety of making mistakes, and immediate feedback. Crucially, simulations helped students visualize abstract concepts like atomic movement.

The researchers concluded that CBS is an effective tool for increasing knowledge and interest by bridging the gap between abstract concepts and visual understanding. Because lower proficiency students showed lower interest, the authors suggest simulations may be more effective as reinforcement tools. They recommend integrating CBS into teaching guides and using simulations for topics that are difficult to visualize or unsafe for traditional labs.
76:
In the article "Student co-creation in an online university: successes, failures and how to move forward," Al Francis D. Librero examines the 2018 Digital Collective initiative at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU). The project aimed to move beyond faculty-centric Open Educational Resources (OERs) by engaging students and alumni to co-create multimedia learning materials, such as graphics, audio, and blogs, to support open educational practice and professional portfolio development.

Using an autoethnographic research method, the author analyzed personal experiences and data from over 30 students and alumni from the Bachelor of Arts in Multimedia Studies program. Findings indicate that while recruitment was successful, most participants remained passive, engaging only through social media "likes" rather than contributing content. This lack of productivity was attributed to competing priorities like work and family, the project's status as an extracurricular activity rather than a curricular one, and a lack of clear organizational hierarchy. Additionally, cultural factors like "hiya" (fear of scrutiny) and a conceptual mismatch—treating a voluntary project as a "learning community" rather than a "community of practice"—hindered progress.

The study concludes that student co-creation requires structural support to compete with other student responsibilities. To move toward productive co-creation, the author recommends clarity of goals, integration into the curriculum via academic credit, formal management structures, capacity building for junior students, and fostering a sense of community.
77:
Dela Cerna, Ibias Jr., and Raymundo investigated maritime students' perceptions of traditional e-Learning versus immersive learning (i-Learning) to address technological gaps in the Philippine maritime education sector. Grounded in Connectivism Theory, the study utilized a quantitative design involving 192 second-year maritime students from the Philippine Merchant Marine Academy. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Multivariate Analysis of Variance (MANOVA) to compare the methods across five dimensions: risk reduction, interactivity, enjoyability, knowledge retention, and applicability to all subjects.

The findings showed that both methods were perceived as most beneficial for time-efficiency. i-Learning was viewed as more realistic and interactive, while e-Learning was considered more cost-effective. Regarding disadvantages, e-Learning was frequently described as boring and non-interactive, whereas i-Learning received much lower negative ratings in these areas. Both methods were perceived as expensive, though e-Learning was rated slightly higher in terms of cost-disadvantage.

MANOVA results indicated no statistically significant difference between traditional e-Learning and i-Learning regarding risk reduction, interactivity, enjoyability, retention, or applicability at an alpha level of 0.05. The researchers concluded that both methods serve as valuable supplemental tools and neither is a complete replacement for the other. They suggest integrating both methods for a balanced environment and recommend that future research include a wider variety of students and objective data on student performance.
78:
Phillip G. Queroda's study, "Massive Open Online Course (MOOC) Readiness of Pangasinan State University – Open University Systems Students," investigates student preparedness for MOOCs as institutions transition toward online delivery. Using a descriptive research method and purposive sampling, the study collected data from 141 respondents. The demographic profile showed that 72.3% were female, 73% were government employees, and most were aged 21 to 30. Notably, 73% of respondents had attended fewer than five seminars regarding online distance education.

Findings indicate varying levels of readiness. Students were considered very much ready in using hardware and standard software like web browsers and Microsoft Office. They demonstrated high readiness in online skills, such as email communication and clerical tasks, as well as in using audio and video media. However, they were only "slightly ready" regarding the use of Learning Management Systems (LMS) and installing specific programs or plugins.

Motivation and engagement levels were high, with students expressing confidence in completing work despite distractions. Students identified frequent participation, prior online experience, immediate application of materials, regular instructor contact, and technical support as vital to success. The study concludes that PSU-OUS students are ready for MOOC implementation. The researcher recommends increased participation in online learning seminars and suggests that the institution pursue MOOCs within the Open Distance Learning framework to support the transition to online delivery.
79:
The rapid evolution of e-learning has increased the demand for high-quality digital materials, such as Learning Objects (LOs). This study evaluated a multimedia LO regarding the "Rotation of Rigid Bodies" in Physics developed by the Interactive Learning Center at the University of the Philippines Los Baños. The research aimed to determine the LO's effect on student knowledge gain and its effectiveness as a supplemental tool based on attractiveness, clarity, applicability, interactivity, and assessment function.

Using a quantitative approach, the study involved 150 students enrolled in a Fundamental Physics 1 course. Participants were divided into a control group receiving standard lectures and a treatment group receiving lectures supplemented by the LO. Findings revealed that the LO significantly enhanced knowledge gain. While both groups improved from pre-test to post-test, the treatment group achieved a significantly higher mean post-test score of 7.80 compared to the control group's 4.23. Socio-demographic characteristics did not significantly affect knowledge gain within the groups.

The LO received high ratings for clarity and comprehensibility (4.38), assessment function (4.28), applicability (4.16), and interactivity (4.14). It received a lower weighted mean for attractiveness (3.86), with suggestions to improve color schemes and graphics. Overall, respondents agreed the LO was an effective supplemental material (4.27). The study concludes that the LO effectively enhances physics knowledge and recommends using LOs to supplement classroom discussions.
86:
The study "Developing Positive Climate and Behavior Management in a Flipped Classroom" examines the implementation of a flipped classroom with peer instruction (FCPI) in a Grade 7 science class in Sta. Cruz, Laguna, Philippines. Using a one-group quasi-experimental design with 47 students, the research investigated how this model affects classroom climate and behavior management. The instructional approach involved asynchronous pre-class activities using DOST science courseware followed by synchronous face-to-face sessions utilizing the Plickers application for real-time formative assessment. Data was gathered through classroom observations, journal entries, and a focus group discussion.

Initial implementation faced challenges such as student disinterest, noise, and lack of engagement. However, as the study progressed, scores in both dimensions increased. The classroom achieved high-range scores in positive affect, relationship, and positive communication, while maintaining middle-range scores for respect. Regarding behavior management, the model reached middle-range scores in clear behavior expectation, proactive management, redirection of misbehavior, and student behavior. Researchers suggested initial unsettledness resulted from the shift from traditional lectures to active learning.

Success was attributed to communicating the model's benefits, arranging the physical layout for collaboration, matching pre-class and in-class activities, and encouraging cooperation. The study concludes that FCPI is an effective framework for 21st-century learning. Recommendations include specific teacher training in technology and activity-based management, providing pre-class materials in Filipino, and using diverse active learning strategies.
87:
The study "Design Research Approach in Developing Technology-Mediated Learning Modules in Practical Mathematics for Technical Vocational Education" addresses the lack of tailored online learning technologies for technical-vocational students in the Philippine K to 12 curriculum, specifically for subjects like Shielded Metal Arc Welding (SMAW). Using the design research model by McKenney and Reeves (2013), researchers employed an iterative methodology to develop and validate design principles for mathematics modules.

The research involved two iterations. The first iteration involved twelve Grade 11 students using modules on unit conversions, algebraic expressions, and ratios/percentages. Following feedback, modules were refined for a second iteration involving twelve Grade 12 students. Findings identified students as ICT-proficient learners who face socio-economic and connectivity challenges. Effective design principles included using small-group collaborative learning through synchronous and asynchronous discussions centered on simplified, authentic, problem-based tasks. Teachers were most effective when acting as facilitators, mentors, and course designers. Facebook was found to be the most effective technology due to its accessibility for messaging and file sharing. Successful module presentation utilized a multimedia approach, including video tutorials, clear text, and practical exercises.

Statistical analysis showed the second iteration group achieved significantly higher mean scores, moving evaluations from "good" to "excellent." The study concludes that technology-mediated modules developed through design research effectively facilitate learning for technical-vocational students.
88:
In the study "Addressing the Needs of Distance Education Learners Based on their Perception of a Successful Student," Mabini DG. Dizon investigates how distance education learners define success and how these perceptions can inform teaching and assessment practices. Conducted at an open education institution in the Philippines, the qualitative study used thematic analysis of graded learning activity reports from 147 learners. The participant profile was predominantly young, female, and single, with 44% being employed.

The findings reveal a significant distinction between student-defined and parent-defined success. A majority of students (70%) define success as the ability to balance academic and non-academic life through discipline and time management, with only 6% equating success solely with high grades. Conversely, 68% of students believe their parents define success through academic excellence at prestigious universities and securing high-paying jobs. While 68% of students believe their friends share their "all-rounder" view of success, 95% of students report being affected by the views of parents and friends. This influence motivates 65% of students but leaves 35% feeling overwhelmed by pressure.

The researcher concludes that student success in distance education is a holistic phenomenon involving social, psychological, and professional dimensions. To support this, the study recommends that faculty provide more synchronous interaction, offer practical and authentic assessments that accommodate diverse circumstances, and streamline module topics to prevent overwhelming workloads.
89:
The COVID-19 pandemic necessitated an unplanned transition from face-to-face instruction to remote learning in the Philippines, raising concerns regarding student welfare and academic integrity. This quantitative study examined the welfare of 25 Bachelor of Arts in Business Economics students at a state university in Pampanga. Using the microeconomic concept of consumer surplus, the researcher treated education as a consumption good, where the "price" included tuition, fees, food, transportation, housing, and internet costs. The study compared students who experienced both face-to-face and remote learning modalities under the same professor during the 2019-2020 and 2020-2021 academic years.

Findings indicated that while willingness to pay and actual costs differed between modalities, the change in consumer surplus was not statistically significant. The mean difference in consumer surplus between face-to-face classes (Php 58,600.00) and remote classes (negative Php 2,520.00) was Php 8,380.00, yielding a p-value of 0.057. However, satisfaction ratings showed a significant difference; students reported a mean satisfaction rating of 4.520 for face-to-face classes, compared to 3.000 for remote classes. Qualitative data identified dissatisfaction due to unfavorable learning environments, lack of interaction, unstable internet, increased course requirements, and less thorough lesson discussions. The study concludes that the shift to remote learning did not significantly impact student welfare as measured by consumer surplus, though pedagogical and environmental challenges persist.
90:
The COVID-19 pandemic forced a global transition from physical classrooms to remote learning in K-12 and tertiary education, requiring institutions to re-evaluate pedagogical frameworks and technology-mediated programs. This special issue examines this shift across various contexts, including technical-vocational, general education, and flipped classroom settings, using methodologies such as design-based research and empirical analysis.

Findings indicate that design-based approaches improve learning experiences in subjects like mathematics. This transition requires teachers to shift from traditional authority figures to facilitators, mentors, and providers of feedback. In online general education, student success is linked to socialization opportunities and timely faculty responses. Therefore, online assessments should prioritize the practical application of knowledge and provide realistic timelines to help students balance academic and non-academic responsibilities.

Regarding student welfare, empirical data suggests the shift to remote learning did not significantly affect welfare. In flipped classroom models, effective behavior management and a positive learning climate require transparency in technology use and face-to-face components that maximize student interaction. Research emphasizes that classroom behavior management is a shared responsibility between teachers and students.

Ultimately, pedagogical roles must adapt to technology-mediated modalities. Teachers must relinquish traditional control over the time and place of learning to empower students. Institutions should train educators to act as facilitators, prioritize practical application in curricula, and implement strategies that promote socialization and transparency to enhance educational quality.
96:
In "A Case Study in Tablet-Based Augmented Reality Vocabulary Acquisition," Adam Dabrowski investigates the efficacy of mobile-based Augmented Reality (AR) for deliberate second language vocabulary acquisition. The study explores whether AR, which overlays digital information onto the real world, facilitates learning more effectively than traditional paper-based word cards, specifically examining the impact of context-independent versus context-dependent scenes.

The methodology utilized a single-subject case study involving a 25-year-old Japanese language teacher with no prior knowledge of Basque. Using three sets of 15 concrete Basque nouns, the study compared three methods: traditional paper-based word cards, context-independent AR (items on a plain white table), and context-dependent AR (items within a familiar desk space). Testing included pretests, posttests, and delayed posttests measuring meaning recognition, form recognition, and form recall.

Findings revealed that both AR methods outperformed paper-based word cards in immediate posttests. The context-dependent AR group achieved the highest immediate score (87%), followed by context-independent AR (80%), while word cards scored 60%. However, in delayed posttests, the context-dependent AR group's scores decayed to 66%, whereas the context-independent AR group and word card group showed unexpected gains or stability, scoring 87% and 66%, respectively. Qualitatively, the participant found AR entertaining and motivating. The study concludes that tablet-based AR is an effective, practical tool for establishing form-meaning links, though further research is needed regarding long-term retention in physical environments.
97:
In the study "Alignment of Teachers’ Epistemic Understanding and Intended Dialogic Scaffolding of Classroom Argumentation: Implications on Face-to-Face, Open and Distance Learning Environments," Sally B. Gutierez examines the relationship between teachers' epistemological beliefs and their use of dialogic scaffolding to support student argumentation in secondary science education in the Philippines. Using a qualitative methodology involving surveys, observations, and interviews with four teachers, the research compared the DepEd curriculum with the PSHS curriculum within biology instruction.

The findings indicate that teachers' levels of epistemic understanding align closely with their intended dialogic scaffolding. The study identified three teacher profiles: highly constructivist, constructivist, and transitional. Highly constructivist teachers utilized a "culture of negotiation," acting as facilitators who used open-ended, higher-level questions and socio-scientific issues to encourage students to defend opinions and build consensus. Conversely, transitional teachers expressed a desire to adopt constructivist practices but remained influenced by traditional, content-heavy approaches, often hindered by time constraints or content knowledge limitations.

The study concludes that epistemic understanding significantly shapes instructional decisions. Teachers who view knowledge as socially constructed are more likely to implement effective scaffolding that enhances student reasoning. The researcher recommends increasing pre-service exposure to inquiry-based approaches and providing continuous professional development to help in-service teachers refine their ability to facilitate classroom argumentation.
98:
April E. Leaño’s study, "Is the University of Makati e-Ready? An Evaluation of Its Faculty’s Technology Acceptance in LMS Utilization," investigates faculty readiness regarding the University of Makati’s (UMak) Learning Management System (LMS), the TBL Hub. Using an explanatory-sequential mixed methods design and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the research evaluated faculty from the College of Education (COE) following the sudden shift to online learning during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The findings indicate that UMak-COE faculty are "e-ready," demonstrating positive technology acceptance. Regarding perceived usefulness, the TBL Hub received a mean score of 2.76, interpreted as "Somewhat Met Expectations." It serves effectively as a repository for teaching materials like syllabi and modules, though it struggles to facilitate online course learning and interaction outside the classroom. Qualitative data highlighted technical issues such as lagging, error messages, and Gradebook difficulties, alongside the major barrier of poor internet connectivity.

Regarding perceived ease of use, the platform received a mean score of 2.97, interpreted as "Agree." Faculty expressed confidence in administrative support and training, despite noting increased preparation time and some resistance to integration. The study concludes that while the TBL Hub is an essential tool for online pedagogy, e-readiness is limited by external connectivity and internal system constraints. Recommendations include upgrading the Moodle system, increasing file upload capacities, and implementing policies to normalize the LMS for all official interactions.
104:
This study investigates the challenges faced by final-year Bachelor of Education students at the University of South Africa, a distance learning institution. The research focuses on students near completion who face high failure rates in the second-level English module, ENG2602. These failures cause despondence and financial strain, particularly for students relying on bursaries. Challenges include the digital divide, limited access to campus resources due to work and family commitments, and the limitations of existing institutional concessions.

Using a mixed-methods approach guided by Keller’s ARCS Model of Motivation, the researcher analyzed data from 200 students. Findings revealed barriers across all four ARCS dimensions: inconsistent internet access (Attention), low self-efficacy due to high-level critical analysis requirements (Confidence), and delayed or vague assignment feedback (Relevance and Satisfaction). Additionally, 36% of students identified the two-hour duration of venue-based examinations as a major barrier for intensive analysis.

To address these issues, the researcher implemented the "Lecturer-in-the-Pocket" (LiP) intervention, utilizing WhatsApp, NoRedInk, and the myUnisa platform to provide mobile-based support. A Portfolio of Evidence (PoE) was also used as a summative assessment to mitigate exam stress. Results showed significant improvement: while 81% of the cohort previously scored between 40% and 49% in traditional exams, 95% of those using the PoE passed the module. The study recommends improving feedback quality, ensuring device access, and allowing alternative assessment formats for students near graduation.
106:
The study "Online Laboratory Instruction as Alternative and Supplementary Mode: Students’ Assessment of the BS Agricultural Biotechnology Program" by Reniel S. Pamplona and Inero V. Ancho examines the effectiveness of remote laboratory instruction for BS ABT students at the University of the Philippines Los Baños during the COVID-19 pandemic. Using a descriptive research design, the researchers surveyed 55 randomly selected students regarding virtual learning access, teaching modes, lecture information, and remote laboratory instruction.

Findings revealed high student satisfaction with faculty teaching styles, course syllabi, learning outcomes, and curriculum coherence. Students also showed high approval for audiovisual presentations, handouts, and course packs. While Google Classroom, Zoom, and Google Meet were the primary tools for asynchronous and synchronous delivery, satisfaction specifically for remote laboratory instruction was low at 45.45%, with 34.55% of students expressing dissatisfaction. Qualitative feedback indicated that while do-it-yourself experiments using household materials allowed for some skill application, students felt a significant lack of hands-on experience with professional equipment, noting that relying on videos and written instructions felt like a waste of specialized training.

The study concludes that online instruction successfully maintained program continuity but serves better as an alternative or supplementary mode rather than a full replacement for physical laboratory work. Researchers recommend that future remote instruction utilize low-cost, accessible materials announced early, provide highly detailed instructions, and implement structured activity sequences.
108:
Junar S. Cano’s study, "A Conjoint Study and Segmentation on the Preferred Online Learning Attributes of Senior High School Learners," examines educational disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Using a quantitative, descriptive, and exploratory design, the researcher sampled 300 senior high school learners from Notre Dame of Marbel University to analyze preferences regarding delivery type, lecture, learning tasks, learning materials, and assessment methods.

Conjoint analysis revealed that assessment methods, specifically multiple-choice and multiple-type exams, were the most significant factor influencing preferences. Other highly valued attributes included synchronous delivery, individual learning tasks, and visual aids, while asynchronous delivery and recorded lectures were less preferred. Socio-demographic data showed most respondents were female, from low-income families, and owned smartphones or laptops, though many faced unreliable internet.

Cluster analysis identified two distinct segments. Segment 1 (54.2%), primarily Grade 12 learners, preferred recorded lectures with slides, individual tasks, hands-on materials, and multiple-choice exams. Segment 2 (45.5%), dominated by Grade 11 learners, preferred live online lectures with slides, reading materials, individual tasks, and multiple-type exams. Chi-square tests confirmed these segments differ significantly in gender, family income, grade level, and internet access. The study concludes that institutions should avoid a "one-size-fits-all" approach, instead prioritizing recorded content for Grade 12 and real-time interaction for Grade 11, while addressing logistical barriers like internet stability.
109:
Lydie D. Paderanga’s qualitative study, "Boundless Classrooms and Touchless Bodies: Teaching Physical Education Online," examines how tertiary physical education (PE) teachers in the Philippines transitioned to remote instruction during the COVID-19 pandemic. Using a phenomenological approach with eight experienced teachers from MSU-Iligan Institute of Technology, the research explores how educators navigated the conflict between contact-heavy PE traditions and social distancing requirements.

Findings reveal that teachers developed innovative pedagogical practices to overcome digital limitations. To replace physical contact, educators utilized demonstration-based instruction via recorded videos. Creative strategies included "TikTok Dance Challenges" and family-involved choreography, while sports management was simulated through e-sports or virtual tournaments. Digital tools like Padlet and social media were employed to manage communication and provide emotional support. These practices were grounded in theories such as Bandura’s Social Learning Theory, Vygotsky’s scaffolding, and Gardner’s Multiple Intelligence Theory.

While teachers viewed their roles as a "calling" and enjoyed fostering student independence, they faced significant obstacles, including poor internet connectivity, lack of gadgets, and power interruptions. Teachers also experienced increased workloads from assessing video outputs. The study concludes that online PE is a viable endeavor, suggesting that learning quality depends more on teacher dedication than the mode of delivery. The author recommends professional development in digital literacy and the development of authentic online assessment tools for future blended learning models.
111:
The article "Google Analytics for User-Centered Design: A Case Study in Open and Distance e-Learning" investigates how web analytics can enhance learner-centered design (LCD) in online and distance education. Because traditional methods often fail to provide data on how students interact with digital resources, the researchers explore how Google Analytics (GA) can inform personalized instructional designs. The study utilizes a student-centered design framework focusing on personalization and localization through the analysis of user parameters.

Using a quantitative, descriptive research design, the authors analyzed one year of anonymized data from an online student support helpdesk system. The findings, based on 155,981 unique users and over 715,052 page views, revealed several critical design factors. Approximately 80% of learners used US-English as their default system setting, and about 80% were located in Pakistan. Regarding technology, more than 60% of learners used the Chrome browser, and users accessed the system via desktops, mobile devices, and tablets. These results emphasize the necessity for English compatibility, cross-browser and cross-OS compatibility, and responsive web design.

The authors conclude that Google Analytics is a significant tool for developing learner-centered interfaces. They suggest that integrating GA with Learning Management Systems and Content Management Systems could allow educators to correlate user behavior with academic performance. Future research should combine GA data with qualitative methods and explore how factors like gender, age, and literacy rates impact learning outcomes.
227:
The study "An Investigation into Learners' Satisfaction in an Online Learning Environment" by Oluniyi Oyeleke and Kayode O. Owoade examines satisfaction levels among online nursing students at Obafemi Awolowo University, Nigeria. As higher education shifts toward digital platforms, understanding learner satisfaction is vital to address challenges like isolation. This research investigates how students perceive the administration and delivery of their programs across four indices: online presence, critical factors for success, learning materials, and learning activities.

The research was conducted at Obafemi Awolowo University, where the Centre for Distance Learning manages programs via the eZone Learning Management System. Using a descriptive survey design and purposive sampling, the authors collected data from 200 and 300-level online nursing students via an adapted Likert-scale questionnaire. Data were analyzed using SPSS, employing frequency distribution, percentage distribution, and mean statistics. In this scoring system, a lower mean value indicates a higher level of satisfaction.

The findings indicate that learners are generally satisfied with the online program (x̅ = 2.046). Students expressed the highest satisfaction with learning materials (x̅ = 1.798) and critical factors for online success (x̅ = 1.89), specifically regarding program content, quality, and learning styles. Regarding learning activities, students reported high satisfaction with quizzes (x̅ = 1.739) and assignments (x̅ = 1.775).

Conversely, significant dissatisfaction was found in several areas. The release of results received the lowest satisfaction rating (x̅ = 2.766), alongside dissatisfaction regarding prompt feedback. Learners were also less satisfied with online presence and the sense of community (x̅ = 2.174), noting difficulty in forming meaningful relationships with peers. Additionally, the frequency of activities like discussion forums and feedback showed lower satisfaction levels than structured assessments.

The study concludes that while instructional content and materials are successful, gaps exist in the social and administrative aspects of the experience. The lack of timely results and perceived lack of instructor presence can lead to isolation. The authors recommend that the CDL implement targeted interventions, such as specialized training
229:
In "Automation in Education with Digital Twins: Trends and Issues," Eric Hawkinson examines the growing application of digital twin technology in education. Digital twins are digital representations that allow seamless data exchange between physical objects and computer-generated counterparts. Originally utilized in manufacturing, these models use sensor data and artificial intelligence to simulate physical behavior with high predictive power.

Through a qualitative literature review and comparative analysis of three use cases—ABBA’s digital avatars, the recreation of actress Carrie Fisher, and a "Dead Professor" scenario in higher education—the author identifies significant trends. These cases highlight the ability to simulate deceased individuals, raising critical questions regarding post-mortem publicity rights, the ownership of lecture recordings, and the likeness rights of educators.

Key features of digital twins include real-time data synchronization, predictive analytics, and dynamic updating. When applied to e-learning, these features can facilitate personalized learning, enhanced virtual reality, real-time feedback, and increased accessibility. However, the technology presents challenges, such as shifting the teacher's role from an information source to a facilitator and the risk of the "obsolescence of analog people." The study concludes that the potential for digital resurrection and automated instruction necessitates proactive regulation, robust security to protect privacy, and legal frameworks to clarify the ownership of digital identities and responsibility for activities attributed to digital twins.
230:
In "Assessing the English Grammar Proficiency of Online Filipino English Teachers," James Michael Pablo investigates declining English proficiency in the Philippines and its implications for the country's competitiveness in the global online English teaching market. As online education increases global competition, the study addresses the tension between high demand for instruction and reported declines in Philippine English proficiency metrics.

Using a descriptive quantitative research design, the study surveyed 401 random Online Filipino English Teachers (OFETs) with at least one year of experience. Participants completed a 40-question multiple-choice grammar placement test via Google Forms, focusing on things, verbs, adjectives, prepositions, and commas.

The findings reveal an overall mean score of 71.23%, indicating significant grammatical weaknesses. Approximately 90% of respondents failed to score above 75%, and only 11% met the 85% threshold required by high-standard online schools. Respondents struggled most with verbs, specifically modals and phrasal verbs, as well as conditionals and prepositions. While proficiency was higher in adjectives and past tense usage with "did," the failure to master fundamental syntactical anchors suggests a gap in language mastery.

The author concludes that this lack of mastery could jeopardize the employability of OFETs and the quality of instruction provided. The study suggests that teachers should engage in proactive training, institutions should implement more stringent hiring and professional development, and national entities must address declining proficiency to maintain the country's reputation.
231:
In the editorial "Extending Realities in Open Distance e-Learning," Roberto B. Figueroa Jr. examines the integration of emerging technologies—such as artificial intelligence, virtual reality, augmented reality, and the metaverse—into educational frameworks. The author argues that while these tools offer immersive potential, they must be implemented without neglecting essential pedagogical concerns or the human dimensions of teaching and learning.

The research, presented through a thematic synthesis of various studies, highlights both the potential and challenges of modernizing ODeL. Regarding immersive technologies, digital twins can provide value through virtual tours and simulations, particularly in STEM courses, though they introduce ethical considerations. Augmented reality was found to be an engaging tool for vocabulary acquisition, offering an interactive way to make language learning more immersive via accessible devices.

Regarding the human dimension, faculty acceptance of Learning Management Systems is a critical indicator of institutional readiness. However, technological readiness is not the sole factor; research highlights concerns regarding the English grammar proficiency of Filipino English teachers and notes that a teacher's epistemic understanding is closely aligned with their ability to use dialogic scaffolding to encourage student participation. The research concludes that while immersive technologies can extend realities, they must be implemented alongside a focus on human elements. Technological competence alone is insufficient; there must be a focus on continuous professional development and pedagogical strategies that support engagement.
243:
Patrick C. De Leon’s study investigates how the COVID-19 pandemic impacted student academic performance and management strategies at a parochial K-12 school in Hermosa, Bataan, Philippines. Using a mixed-methods design, the research compared the weighted average grades of 49 Grade 10 students from the pre-pandemic year to the first two years of the pandemic. Qualitative data was collected through surveys and interviews with 35 staff members to determine if the school's response was driven by its Catholic identity or formal administrative mandates.

Findings showed no significant difference in student grades between the pre-pandemic year and the first year of the pandemic, but a significant difference emerged by the second year of the pandemic. Despite statistical shifts, qualitative respondents rated student performance as "very good," noting high grades and active participation. To maintain instruction, the school implemented blended learning, provided printed modules, and monitored student progress.

The study found that the school's management was primarily guided by formal government memoranda from the Department of Education rather than its Catholic identity. Only 28.5% of respondents indicated that religious or school officials guided their measures, suggesting that formal management models take precedence during crises. Challenges included poor internet connectivity, home distractions, and difficulties verifying work in printed modules. The author recommends preparing formal management structures for future disruptions and creating "learning commons" to assist students facing the digital divide.
249:
Martin Jerome G. Goli-Cruz investigated how higher education faculty at a state university in the Philippines perceive the use of ChatGPT in academic settings. The study explored how faculty attitudes toward this artificial intelligence tool influence educational approaches and its potential to drive social transformation, addressing the tension between fostering student-centered learning and risks to academic integrity and cognitive development. Using a qualitative approach with 20 faculty members, data were collected via an online survey and an interview with an AI in education expert, then analyzed using exploratory qualitative and thematic analysis.

Findings revealed multifaceted perceptions. Faculty recognized ChatGPT as a beneficial instructional tool for generating data, creating templates, reviewing essays, and providing immediate feedback. It was viewed as a potential automated tutor that could streamline administrative tasks and provide alternative engagement for introverted students. Conversely, skepticism was high due to limited knowledge, lack of training, and inadequate access. Key concerns included academic dishonesty, misinformation, and student overreliance, which might hinder the development of critical thinking, analytical, and evaluative skills.

While ChatGPT can facilitate advanced learning techniques and classroom discourse, its efficacy depends on guiding students to use it to enhance rather than replace cognitive processes. The study concludes ChatGPT is a "double-edged sword." Institutions must establish ethical guidelines, provide formal training, and reassess assessment protocols to ensure AI enhances human abilities rather than diminishing fundamental cognitive processes.
250:
In the article "ChatGPT — A Threat or an Aid in Teaching and Learning," Magtoto, Bagnol, and Abunda investigate whether Generative Pre-trained Transformers serve as beneficial tools or threats to traditional pedagogy. Grounded in Web 3.0, Bandura’s theory of reciprocal determinism, and Constructivism, the study utilized exploratory and analytical methods. Researchers conducted a literature review and tested ChatGPT’s intellectual capabilities using International Baccalaureate past papers in Chemistry, Biology, Physics, and Mathematics. These responses were categorized by Bloom’s Taxonomy and evaluated by tenured subject teachers against official marking schemes.

The findings revealed varied proficiency levels based on subject and task complexity. In Chemistry, ChatGPT was proficient at lower-level tasks like balancing equations but struggled with higher-level analysis. Biology results were mixed, providing detailed answers for some complex processes but failing to include all necessary points in other descriptive questions. Physics results were generally positive, with the AI providing concise, correct answers for conceptual and calculation-based questions. However, performance in Mathematics was the weakest, as the AI consistently failed to provide correct numerical answers or matching working solutions.

The study concludes that while ChatGPT can act as a conversational tutor, it cannot substitute for human educators. The researchers recommend an "AI-empowered" model focusing on responsible integration rather than bans. They suggest redesigning assessments to include tasks AI cannot replicate, such as creating diagrams, and implementing policies regarding data privacy, academic honesty, and equitable access.
254:
In the article "Learning Transitions in Studying Development: Design, Methodologies/Approaches, Tools in the Digital and Hybrid Platforms," Alexander Michael Palma examines the evolution of educational modalities in the post-pandemic era, specifically within Development Studies. The research addresses the need to reconfigure traditional settings to mitigate risks like limited mobility and restricted resource access. In this discipline, pandemic constraints make translating theory into field application difficult, while a digital divide creates disparities in access to online learning.

The study focuses on the transition from purely online instruction to hybrid models at the Asian Center of the University of the Philippines during the 2022-2023 academic year. Using qualitative analysis of five specific courses, the research evaluated 16 students based on participation, interactions, and written outputs.

Findings indicate that hybrid learning effectiveness varies by discipline. Course design must be dynamic; for instance, case studies work well for in-person discussions, while policy literature analysis suits online presentation. While online environments allow for visual supplements, hybrid models offer superior opportunities for peer-to-peer interaction and social identity building, which helps mitigate the isolation of distance education.

The author concludes that hybrid learning is an inevitable feature of future education. Success requires a tripartite effort from learners, instructors, and institutions. Institutions must invest in infrastructure and staff capacity-building, while instructors should utilize multimedia tools creatively. Finally, institutions should institutionalize evaluations based on student feedback and academic outcomes.
257:
Rapid technological transformation and global health emergencies have shifted tertiary education toward integrated, hybrid, and blended learning models. This study investigated an enhanced Digital Communication course designed for Liberal Arts students to meet post-pandemic digital needs. Using a quantitative causal and comparative research design, researchers surveyed 152 first-year students at Rajamangala University of Technology Rattanakosin in February 2023. The study examined how perceived prior digital technology knowledge influences perceived cognitive learning acquisition and explored differences in learning acquisition among students in English, Chinese, and Japanese language programs.

Findings indicate that students' perceived prior digital technology knowledge significantly influences their perceived cognitive learning acquisition. Students with strong foundational knowledge in areas like internet connectivity and social media management demonstrated higher cognitive learning, including better understanding of digital device management and communication methods. Significant differences in perceived learning acquisition were found across the English, Chinese, and Japanese language groups regarding cognitive, affective, and psychomotor domains. All three groups reported high levels of affective learning acquisition, specifically in areas such as collaboration, digital citizenship, netiquette, and confidence.

The study concludes the course successfully utilized an ergonomic approach to facilitate active and constructive learning. Results suggest students have become "novice digital resilient," developing necessary self-regulation for online environments. Researchers recommend offering prerequisite computer basics courses and suggest future qualitative studies to provide more nuanced discussions.
261:
Cerdeña, Mangubat, Gelisan, and Crisanto investigated quality assurance in the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) MOOC "Principles of Graphic Design." Using Biggs’ 3P Model, the researchers focused on the "product" variable to assess learning outcomes. The methodology combined Learning Management System (LMS) analytics with a Qualtrics survey based on the Commonwealth of Learning’s guidelines. The study analyzed a sample of 7,239 learners from an initial enrollment of 22,942 students.

The findings revealed high success across measured variables. The course achieved a 33.21% completion rate, with 7,620 students receiving certificates. Learner enjoyment was overwhelmingly positive regarding outcomes perception, continuing education, and employment opportunities, all scoring above 4.0. The socializing dimension was the only area receiving a neutral rating. Regarding self-satisfaction, 77.95% of respondents reported being "very satisfied," with the highest ratings attributed to course materials, followed by the teacher/coordinator, assessment, and learner support. Qualitative feedback described materials as "helpful" and "useful," and instructors as "informative."

The study concludes the MOOC is highly effective in terms of enjoyment, satisfaction, and completion. Results suggest learners prioritize practical knowledge over social interaction. Researchers suggest improving the socializing component through collaborative activities to foster 21st-century skills. This study provides a validated methodology for post-delivery evaluation and suggests future research into the relationship between enrollment intentions and completion rates.
264:
In "Engendering Agency, Mindfulness, and Critical Thinking in Online Education," Tina S. Clemente examines pedagogical shifts required by the transition to online graduate education at the University of the Philippines Diliman's Asian Center. The study investigates the difficulty of fostering agency, mindfulness, and critical thinking within an online modality that intensifies socio-economic and personal pressures. Focusing on the Asian Studies 230 Seminar from 2020 to 2022, the researcher utilized phenomenography to observe a "Discussion Program" (DP) designed to replace passive reporting with interactive, student-led engagement.

Findings indicate that the DP positively impacted learning by shifting toward relational and reciprocal practices. Student leaders achieved subject matter mastery through "learning by teaching," while the cohort experienced increased active engagement and community building. Creative framing encouraged students to reimagine problems and meanings. However, challenges emerged, such as students struggling to move beyond the "inertia of routine" and the difficulty of maintaining relational components due to the inherent distance of online education and students keeping cameras off.

External barriers significantly impacted engagement, including unequal access to devices and internet, inadequate physical spaces, and the psycho-emotional effects of isolation. Digital fatigue and multitasking between work and studies often led students to rely on "stock knowledge" rather than higher-order thinking. The author concludes that online education requires educators to view the development of these competencies as an iterative process of design and adjustment.
265:
The study "Improving Tertiary Students’ Academic Performance and Appreciation of the Life and Works of Jose Rizal Course through Digital-based Biographical Museum Simulation" addresses student disengagement in history-based courses. Despite mandates to teach Jose Rizal's life to instill nationalism, students often find the subject boring and rely on rote memorization. To address this, researchers developed a digital-based biographical museum simulation designed to provide an interactive, immersive, and multisensory experience.

Using a quasi-experimental and qualitative approach, the researchers studied 50 college students from Kolehiyo ng Lungsod ng Dasmariñas. Participants were divided into an experimental group, which used a digital museum simulation featuring eight stories of Rizal’s life, and a comparison group following the standard syllabus. Data were collected through pre-tests, formative tests, post-tests, and focus-group discussions.

Findings revealed that the digital simulation positively impacted academic performance. While both groups had a "low" pre-test mean score of 12.40, the experimental group showed a significantly higher increase of 6.96 points compared to the comparison group's 4.08-point increase. Although post-test mean scores were not statistically significantly different, the experimental group consistently outperformed the comparison group in formative assessments. Qualitative data showed improved appreciation, as the multisensory nature of the tool sustained interest and aided retention. The study concludes the simulation is an effective tool for improving performance and appreciation by overcoming the limitations of static teaching methods.
266:
The study "Quality of Study Life During the COVID-19 Pandemic of UPLB Students" investigated the remote distance learning (RDL) experiences of 350 students at the University of the Philippines Los Baños. Using the Four Pillars of Supporting Student Success framework, the researchers analyzed the impact of the transition from face-to-face to online instruction on academic support, technology, health, and community. Due to a low response rate, the findings apply only to the non-probability sample.

The majority of respondents were female and aged 18 to 24. Most students used smartphones and laptops to access materials via Learning Management Systems, though many reported limited access to physical library resources. Female respondents reported higher comfort levels with RDL and fewer concerns regarding data privacy compared to males.

Mental health challenges were significant, with many students reporting a loss of motivation and uncertainty about the future. Academics, specifically workload and perceived lack of professor consideration, was the primary stressor for both genders. Females reported additional stressors, including domestic obligations and difficulty accessing resources. While most felt supported by family, only 50% felt the university provided sufficient support or that they belonged to their college community.

The researchers recommend a holistic approach to student success. Suggestions include increasing information on digital library services, providing more training on LMS and data privacy, and expanding gender-sensitive counseling services. They also suggest considering familial obligations in scholarship criteria and exploring hybrid learning models.
268:
The study "Towards an Age-friendly University: An Intergenerational Study among FICS-UPOU Graduates" examines the educational experiences of graduates from the Faculty of Information and Communication Studies at the University of the Philippines Open University for the 2017-2018 academic year. Aligned with the Age-Friendly University Global Network, the research investigates whether the university's instructional design and curriculum facilitate inclusive, intergenerational learning within an open and distance e-Learning context.

The methodology involved surveying graduates from five FICS programs, categorized into Baby Boomers, Generation X, and Millennials. The assessment evaluated curriculum relevance, program usefulness, quality of instruction, effectiveness of online delivery, and current employability. Findings indicated that the majority of respondents were Millennials, followed by Generation X and Baby Boomers. Overall, respondents reported a highly positive learning experience, with the highest mean score attributed to program usefulness and the lowest to the effectiveness of online delivery.

Statistical analysis revealed that gender and age group were not significantly associated with the learning experience, suggesting the curriculum is age-friendly across generations. However, employment status showed a significant, weak inverse correlation with both the effectiveness of online delivery and current employability, indicating that full-time employment may present challenges.
